title: Measuring iron with visible light
section: What number are we trying to report?
text:
What number are we trying to report?

From the supplied water sample through preparation, calibration, and checking to a reported concentration.mg elemental Fe/L in the supplied filtered water. What must be true before that number is meaningful?

Ask students to distinguish a signal from a chemical result. The waters are simulated, filtered and fortified. Assume all dissolved iron is quantitatively reduced and complexed, with no loss. This is not a digestion or total-recovery claim for arbitrary environmental water. The full unit and project are linked from the course home page.

title: Measuring iron with visible light
text:
Chemistry creates the absorber

Fe²⁺ plus three phenanthroline ligands forms the red-orange iron complex.Reduction, acidity, and excess ligand affect the amount of coloured complex.

Phen means 1,10-phenanthroline. Each ligand is bidentate. The diagram illustrates stoichiometry, not geometry. Ask what incomplete reduction would do to the result. Do not equate measured iron after reduction with original Fe(II). Background: https://staff.buffalostate.edu/nazareay/che301/l9.pdf .

title: Measuring iron with visible light
text:
Follow the light

Selected light enters a one-centimetre cuvette. The detector measures the transmitted light relative to the reference.The reference is a reagent blank. These files are already blank-referenced.

I zero is the matched reference intensity; I is transmitted intensity through the prepared sample. Discuss the purpose of a reagent blank and why a further subtraction changes an already referenced measurement. Compare an empty cell, solvent reference, and a matched reagent blank verbally.

title: Measuring iron with visible light
text:
Why choose 510 nm?

The simulated iron-standard spectrum peaks near 510 nm and the reagent-blank response is small.A strong response and a flat local maximum help. Does the maximum prove selectivity?

It does not: other components may absorb. These curves are a simulated Gaussian envelope, not authentic identification spectra. Rows are wavelengths within a scan, not independent replicates. Connect to the known approximate visible maximum of the iron(II) complex; the university example uses 508 nm.

title: Measuring iron with visible light
text:
Absorbance and concentration
\[A=-\log_{10}(I/I_0), \qquad A=\varepsilon l c\]
At fixed wavelength and path, a suitable dilute solution gives a proportional response. Our calibration uses mg Fe/L, not mol/L.
Predict: if \(T=0.50\), \(A\approx0.301\). If absorbance doubles, what happens to transmittance?

Transmittance becomes approximately 0.25. Emphasise that doubling absorbance squares transmittance. We use an empirical calibration slope in L/mg Fe, not a molar absorptivity. Chemical equilibrium, stray light, and excessive absorbance can break a simple linear relationship.

title: Measuring iron with visible light
text:
Fit what we measured

Standards between zero and four mg Fe/L and their fitted absorbance response.lm(absorbance ~ standard_mg_l, data = standards)

Retrieve the earlier calibration lesson. Eighteen independent final standard solutions, three per concentration, are measured once each. The unweighted line retains its intercept: a=0.003873883 and b=0.198799368. Do not force zero or reverse the regression. Units of slope are L/mg Fe.

title: Measuring iron with visible light
section: A good line needs a diagnostic
text:
A good line needs a diagnostic

Residual absorbance versus concentration; no obvious curvature in this teaching dataset.What would curvature mean? What could small residuals still fail to reveal?

Inspect curvature, spread and unusual points. The assumptions are constant response variance and negligible standard concentration uncertainty. Small residuals cannot validate recovery or sample-specific interferences. Do not remove inconvenient observations simply to improve the fit.

title: Measuring iron with visible light
text:
What counts as replication?

One collected water sample gives two independent preparations, each measured three times.Six readings are not six independently collected waters.

P01 and P02 share W1. Repeated readings describe reading repeatability; preparing another aliquot probes additional variation. Both still use the same calibration. Do not divide every contribution by the square root of six.

title: Measuring iron with visible light
text:
Match by preparation ID
means |>
  left_join(preparations, by = "preparation_id")

Require one preparation record per ID.
Require a preparation record for every measured ID.
Inspect the joined rows and units.

The two CSV files deliberately have different row orders.

This is the principal new table operation. Have students predict the error from joining by row position. The lesson includes stopifnot checks for unique keys and complete matches. Row order has no chemical meaning.

title: Measuring iron with visible light
text:
Correct the preparation factor

Ten millilitres made up to a total of fifty millilitres gives a factor of five.P01: \(\bar A=0.480620\) → 2.398 mg Fe/L final → 11.99 mg Fe/L original.

Invert A=a+bc, then multiply by final volume over aliquot volume. Total final volume includes reagents. Keep all numerical precision in code. State the concentration basis: elemental iron in the original supplied filtered water.

title: Measuring iron with visible light
section: An old out-of-range reading needs new evidence
text:
An old out-of-range reading needs new evidence

P03 lies beyond the standard range; the newly prepared and measured P04 lies within it.P04 uses a new 5.00 mL aliquot, made to 50.00 mL. Its result is about 27.00 mg Fe/L original.

P03 mean A=1.07507 exceeds the validated teaching range. P04 mean A=0.54061 is within range; its factor is 10. Editing the dilution factor on P03 cannot create a new measurement. Crosses on this illustration locate response levels using the line’s algebraic inverse; unsupported values are not exported as results.

title: Measuring iron with visible light
text:
Independent QC can stop reporting

Independent QC recovers about 99.6 percent in block A and 85.2 percent in later block B; only A meets the exercise criterion.Withhold P05 from block B. Investigate and remeasure after satisfactory QC.

Acceptance is a supplied 95–105 percent recovery window for this exercise. Calibration from A is checked before use in later B. Do not retroactively invalidate A or automatically correct B by dividing by the failed QC recovery. QC failure signals a problem but does not identify the cause.

title: Measuring iron with visible light
text:
Uncertainty survives averaging

Illustrative P01 standard uncertainty contributions: calibration and readings, final volume, and aliquot volume.P01: 11.991 mg Fe/L; standard uncertainty 0.028 mg Fe/L under the stated model.

The supplied helper includes response and slope/intercept uncertainty through a first-order inverse-calibration calculation. Independent volume uncertainties are added by root-sum-of-squares. This is not a 95 percent half-width. Sampling, recovery, matrix bias and standard concentration uncertainty are omitted. The approximate 95 percent interval 2.3886–2.4077 applies only to final solution concentration before volume uncertainty is added.

title: Measuring iron with visible light
text:
Transfer the reasoning
A new preparation uses 2.00 mL made up to 50.00 mL, measured in accepted block A. Readings: 0.399, 0.401, 0.400.

Check the mean and range.
Estimate the final concentration.
Apply the preparation factor.
State what is missing from a full uncertainty statement.


Mean=0.400; final estimate=1.9925924 mg Fe/L; factor=25; original estimate=49.8148 mg Fe/L. The proposed point answer is 49.81. It does not have an evaluated preparation uncertainty because new volume uncertainties were not supplied.

Rebuild the whole argument

Analytical workflow from a defined question through preparation and checks to a result with uncertainty.Render your R Markdown report from a fresh session. Include the chemical assumptions and reasons for every withheld result.

Students should retain source, data, output CSV and HTML. Ask which error no amount of R code can repair without new chemical evidence. Examples: failed recovery or an old saturated reading. Refer to the full lesson for hints.

title: Separation principles
section: A detector sees what arrives together
text:
A detector sees what arrives together

A snapshot shows two separated bands moving through a column. The less retained band is further towards the outlet; time-resolved detection gives peaks.How can we make a mixed response more selective?

Separate components in time before detection. Retention and width both matter; a detector need not distinguish every coeluting compound.

title: Separation principles
section: A column snapshot is not a chromatogram
text:
A column snapshot is not a chromatogram

A snapshot shows two separated bands moving through a column. The less retained band is further towards the outlet; time-resolved detection gives peaks.This picture is position inside a column at one time.

The less retained band is further towards the outlet. A chromatogram instead measures the outlet response across time.

title: Separation principles
text:
Repeated exchange controls average migration

Solutes repeatedly exchange between mobile and stationary phases. A greater stationary-phase residence fraction delays average migration.Solute moves while it occupies the mobile phase.

Greater stationary-phase residence slows average migration. This is a conceptual equilibrium picture, not a statement that molecules stop exchanging.

title: Separation principles
text:
Interactions create retention and selectivity

Solutes repeatedly exchange between mobile and stationary phases. A greater stationary-phase residence fraction delays average migration.Conditions can change the relative residence of two compounds.

Mobile-phase composition, stationary phase and temperature can affect the balance differently for different solutes.

title: Separation principles
text:
Read the chromatogram axes

A simulated chromatogram has unretained time one minute and resolved component peaks near three and four minutes.Response versus elapsed run time.

One row is a time position within a run, not an independently collected sample. Many CSV rows do not supply many independent replicates.

title: Separation principles
text:
Identify the transit time

A simulated chromatogram has unretained time one minute and resolved component peaks near three and four minutes.The dashed marker is \(t_0=1.00\) min.

It represents unretained transit, not an analyte peak. Distinguish the marker from the measured components.

title: Separation principles
text:
Subtract transit before calculating retention

A simulated chromatogram has unretained time one minute and resolved component peaks near three and four minutes.\(k=(t_R-t_0)/t_0\).

For peak A at three minutes, k is two, not three. The factor is dimensionless when times use matching units.

title: Separation principles
text:
Compare the two retention factors

A simulated chromatogram has unretained time one minute and resolved component peaks near three and four minutes.A: \(k=2\); B: \(k=3\); selectivity \(\alpha=1.5\).

Both k and alpha refer to the stated conditions. Greater retention alone is not a promise of useful separation.

title: Separation principles
section: Peak area and height are different quantities
text:
Peak area and height are different quantities

Broader component peaks overlap more despite unchanged retention times and component areas.Which can remain the same while a peak becomes lower?

Integrated area can stay constant when a fixed amount is spread over a longer time, under a stable linear response and correct baseline.

title: Separation principles
section: Calibration still supplies the amount relation
text:
Calibration still supplies the amount relation

A simulated chromatogram has unretained time one minute and resolved component peaks near three and four minutes.A larger peak is not a universal count of molecules.

Response factor, introduced amount and detector selectivity matter. A standard calibrates under defined conditions.

title: Separation principles
text:
Resolution includes spacing and width
\(R_s=2(t_{R2}-t_{R1})/(w_1+w_2)\).

These widths are baseline widths, not half-height widths. Keep all time units consistent.

title: Separation principles
text:
Calculate the resolved pair

A simulated chromatogram has unretained time one minute and resolved component peaks near three and four minutes.2 × (4.0 − 3.0)/(0.4 + 0.5) = 2.222.

Require students to identify widths and retention times from the supplied peak summary.

title: Separation principles
text:
A familiar threshold needs conditions

A simulated chromatogram has unretained time one minute and resolved component peaks near three and four minutes.Near 1.5 can be useful for similar Gaussian peaks; adequacy depends on the task.

Unequal peak amounts, tailing and interference can make one threshold insufficient. Do not declare purity from the number alone.

title: Separation principles
text:
Changed spacing reduces resolution

The same component areas appear resolved or overlapping when their retention-time spacing changes.The overlap run has \(R_s=0.667\).

Both component areas are unchanged in the simulated model. A combined detector response can now be difficult to assign.

title: Separation principles
section: An integration boundary is not chemical selectivity
text:
An integration boundary is not chemical selectivity

The same component areas appear resolved or overlapping when their retention-time spacing changes.Does drawing a split recover independent evidence?

No: assigning a combined response to components requires a justified model or additional evidence. A vertical split alone can create misleading precision.

title: Separation principles
text:
Changed width also reduces resolution

Broader component peaks overlap more despite unchanged retention times and component areas.The broad run keeps retention times but has \(R_s=0.909\).

This shows why retention time differences alone do not guarantee adequate separation.

title: Separation principles
text:
Separate efficiency from selectivity

A snapshot shows two separated bands moving through a column. The less retained band is further towards the outlet; time-resolved detection gives peaks.Narrower bands and different relative retention solve different problems.

A more efficient column cannot always rescue unsuitable phase selectivity. Discuss injection and extra-column dispersion as other width sources.

title: Separation principles
section: Estimate plate efficiency only with a stated model
text:
Estimate plate efficiency only with a stated model
For ideal Gaussian peaks, \(N=16(t_R/w_b)^2\).

Use the baseline-width version with its assumptions. Half-height widths require the appropriate coefficient. Do not swap export columns silently.

title: Separation principles
section: Why can very slow flow broaden bands?
text:
Why can very slow flow broaden bands?

A dimensionless illustrative plate-height curve is high at both low and high mobile-phase velocity.Diffusion acts over a longer time.

Use the low-velocity region of the illustrative H=A+B/u+Cu curve. Values are dimensionless and not measured instrument settings.

title: Separation principles
section: Why can very fast flow broaden bands?
text:
Why can very fast flow broaden bands?

A dimensionless illustrative plate-height curve is high at both low and high mobile-phase velocity.Finite mass transfer can prevent efficient exchange.

Use the high-velocity region. An apparent optimum depends on column and method; pressure and run time matter too.

title: Separation principles
section: Identity needs more than expected retention
text:
Identity needs more than expected retention

The same component areas appear resolved or overlapping when their retention-time spacing changes.Another component can arrive at the same time.

A reference standard, method consistency and additional selective evidence can strengthen assignment. Coelution can remain hidden.

title: Separation principles
text:
Transfer the definitions

Broader component peaks overlap more despite unchanged retention times and component areas.t₀=0.80; tR=2.40 and 3.20; baseline widths=0.40 and 0.60 min.

Answers k one two, k two three, alpha one point five, resolution one point six. Ask how doubling both widths changes resolution: halves it, without changing k or alpha.

title: Separation principles
section: Choose the next action from the failure
text:
Choose the next action from the failure

Solutes repeatedly exchange between mobile and stationary phases. A greater stationary-phase residence fraction delays average migration.Is it spacing, width, identity evidence or calibration that is missing?

Avoid a generic change-everything response. Match a proposed measurement or method adjustment to the observed limitation.

title: From sample to answer
section: A number needs a chemical question
text:
A number needs a chemical question

Four parts of a measurand: analyte and matrix, material scope, quantity and unit, and procedure.What quantity will our result describe?

Ask for quantity, material scope and unit before naming an instrument. Use a bottle of water as the concrete example.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Separate analyte from matrix

A selective chloride procedure and conductivity do not have the same measurand.Chloride is the analyte. Water and other dissolved components form the matrix.

The matrix is not necessarily inert. It can change selectivity, recovery or response.

title: From sample to answer
section: The same sample can answer different questions
text:
The same sample can answer different questions

A selective chloride procedure and conductivity do not have the same measurand.Conductivity and chloride concentration are different measurands.

Ask whether higher conductivity proves more chloride. Several mobile ionic species contribute. A calibration for one property cannot be transferred without a chemical relation.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Include place and time

Four parts of a measurand: analyte and matrix, material scope, quantity and unit, and procedure.A result from the supplied bottle is not automatically a river-wide mean.

Ask students what claim is justified if all material came from a single location at one time. This introduces sampling without inventing a representative design.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Preparation belongs in the definition

The result applies to a defined material under a defined procedure; the signal alone does not define the measurand.Filtered iron, unfiltered iron and original Fe(II) need different evidence.

Filtration changes material entering the procedure; reduction changes species. Later lessons will make the assumptions explicit.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Qualitative and quantitative claims
Identity: what evidence supports the substance?
Amount: what relates the selective response to a quantity?

A peak at an expected retention time is evidence, but coelution is possible. Amount needs both identification/selectivity and a suitable response calibration.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Follow the result backwards

The result applies to a defined material under a defined procedure; the signal alone does not define the measurand.Which record connects this reported concentration to the collected material?

Trace question, collected sample, preparation, signal, calibration and back-calculation. R cannot repair a missing preparation record.

title: From sample to answer
section: One row means one collected sample
text:
One row means one collected sample

Eight collected waters show inlet chloride of 18–21 mg/L and outlet chloride of 11–14 mg/L.Eight rows: four inlet samples and four outlet samples.

These are simulated independent collected samples in the teaching design. They are not before/after pairs merely because row positions can be matched.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Retrieve the familiar import
water <- read_csv("data/course/water.csv")
glimpse(water)

Check types, IDs, units, missing values and the experimental unit. Keep raw data unchanged. Use the R project to establish relative paths.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Show the observations first

Eight collected waters show inlet chloride of 18–21 mg/L and outlet chloride of 11–14 mg/L.What is the difference between the locations? What variation remains?

Means are 19.5 and 12.5 mg/L. Individual observations make sample size and spread visible. Do not jump to a p-value.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Summarise with a count
water |> group_by(location) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_mg_l = mean(chloride_mg_l))

Read the numerical means as summaries of four collected samples each. A count of missing results would also be necessary in incomplete data.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Make a restrained claim

Eight collected waters show inlet chloride of 18–21 mg/L and outlet chloride of 11–14 mg/L.The descriptive difference is 7.0 mg/L for these samples.

Ask what additional sampling would support a broader temporal or spatial claim. The available design does not establish a treatment effect.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Concentration is amount per volume

Taking a larger volume increases the collected mass at unchanged concentration, assuming a homogeneous solution.\(c=m/V\); therefore \(m=cV\).

Before revealing the example, ask whether taking a larger volume changes concentration or collected amount. Assume a homogeneous solution.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Calculate the collected amount

Taking a larger volume increases the collected mass at unchanged concentration, assuming a homogeneous solution.20.0 mg/L × 0.250 L = 5.00 mg.

Cancel litres explicitly. At unchanged concentration, a half-litre portion would contain ten milligrams.

title: From sample to answer
section: Convert the unit and the number together
text:
Convert the unit and the number together
20 mg/L = 0.020 g/L.

A thousand-fold conversion error is not fixed by additional decimal places. Keep units in labels and the dictionary.

title: From sample to answer
section: A different graph answers a different question
text:
A different graph answers a different question

Calculated chloride amount in equal quarter-litre collected samples, retaining each sample ID.This axis is amount in a collected portion, not concentration.

All portions are 0.250 L here. If volumes varied, amount comparisons could differ from concentration comparisons.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Keep evidence portable

The result applies to a defined material under a defined procedure; the signal alone does not define the measurand.Raw data → saved code → derived table → rendered report.

Restart R and render. A console-only object makes a report dependent on session history. Reproducibility preserves reasoning; it does not guarantee the reasoning is correct.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Transfer: a new portion

Taking a larger volume increases the collected mass at unchanged concentration, assuming a homogeneous solution.0.0750 mg in 25.00 mL. What is the concentration?

Allow a calculation before answering: 3.00 mg/L. Then ask what is missing for a location-wide mean and an uncertainty statement.

title: From sample to answer
section: What would make this conclusion wrong?
text:
What would make this conclusion wrong?
Name one sampling, chemical and computing failure.

Possible answers: top-only sampling; nonspecific response; wrong volume unit or unmatched preparation record. Recover the whole argument, not a list of commands.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: Why can a good external line give a low result?
text:
Why can a good external line give a low result?

Sample-matrix sensitivity is about 0.1496 response units per mg/L, below the external-standard slope of 0.1998.The sample changes the response per unit analyte.

Introduce multiplicative matrix suppression. A correct fit in simple solvent is not evidence that sensitivity is unchanged in sample.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Separate multiplicative and additive effects

Sample-matrix sensitivity is about 0.1496 response units per mg/L, below the external-standard slope of 0.1998.Changed sensitivity and unrelated background are different problems.

Standard addition can address some sensitivity differences; it does not automatically subtract an unknown interferent.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
A spike tests incremental response

Adding 1.00 mg/L increases the external estimate by 0.75 mg/L, giving 75 percent incremental recovery.What should adding a known amount change?

The increase, after matched dilution and preparation, should reflect the supplied analyte increment under the method assumptions.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: Put all terms on the same volume basis
text:
Put all terms on the same volume basis

Five flasks have equal sample aliquots and equal final volume, but increasing standard additions expressed as final-flask concentration.Both final flasks have the same sample fraction and total volume.

If volumes differ, raw concentration differences can mix dilution with recovery. Here added concentration is explicitly final-flask concentration.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Calculate the observed recovery

Adding 1.00 mg/L increases the external estimate by 0.75 mg/L, giving 75 percent incremental recovery.Estimate rises from 1.50 to 2.25 mg/L after adding 1.00 mg/L.

The incremental recovery is seventy-five percent. State that no universal acceptance window is supplied for all matrices.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Interpret 75% correctly

Added analyte may not behave like native bound analyte. A successful late spike cannot establish complete extraction of native material.It is evidence about the added analyte from its addition point onward.

It does not prove that every native analyte molecule experiences exactly the same loss.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: A late addition misses early extraction losses
text:
A late addition misses early extraction losses

Added analyte may not behave like native bound analyte. A successful late spike cannot establish complete extraction of native material.Which step did the spike not pass through?

A post-extraction spike cannot establish extraction recovery. Even a pre-extraction free spike may differ from native bound analyte.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Build a fixed-volume standard-addition series

Five flasks have equal sample aliquots and equal final volume, but increasing standard additions expressed as final-flask concentration.Every flask: 10.00 mL sample made to 25.00 mL.

Vary standard addition, not the final matrix fraction. Added concentration is expressed in the final flask.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: Write the sample contribution in the final flask
text:
Write the sample contribution in the final flask

Five flasks have equal sample aliquots and equal final volume, but increasing standard additions expressed as final-flask concentration.\(c_{native,final}=c_s V_s/V_f\).

The original sample is diluted to forty percent of its original concentration. This contribution remains the same across flasks.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
State the response model
\(y=b(c_sV_s/V_f+c_{added,final})\).

Background has already been corrected. Sensitivity is assumed constant across flasks and equal for native and added analyte. The model, not the graph alone, enables inference.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Fit the familiar straight line

Blank-corrected response rises with final-flask added analyte; the intercept includes native sample analyte.lm(blank_corrected_signal ~ spike_mg_l_final, data = additions)

Reuse lm. The new idea is the experimental design and chemical meaning of its intercept.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Read the slope

Sample-matrix sensitivity is about 0.1496 response units per mg/L, below the external-standard slope of 0.1998.Matrix slope ≈ 0.1496, versus external ≈ 0.1998.

Units are signal units per mg/L. The sample suppresses response in the teaching model.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Read the intercept

Blank-corrected response rises with final-flask added analyte; the intercept includes native sample analyte.Response at zero added analyte ≈ 0.3004.

Zero added analyte still leaves native analyte in every sample aliquot. This is not the same as a zero-analyte blank.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Locate the negative intercept

The standard-addition line extrapolates to a negative x-intercept near minus 2.008 mg/L in the final flask.\(x_0=-a/b\approx-2.0080\) mg/L.

It is a model-based extrapolation. No negative solution is prepared.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: Undo the dilution of the sample aliquot
text:
Undo the dilution of the sample aliquot

Five flasks have equal sample aliquots and equal final volume, but increasing standard additions expressed as final-flask concentration.2.0080 × 25.00/10.00 = 5.020 mg/L original.

The magnitude of the intercept refers to the final flask. Omitting the volume correction leaves the wrong sample basis.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Compare external calibration

Sample-matrix sensitivity is about 0.1496 response units per mg/L, below the external-standard slope of 0.1998.The external answer is about 3.761 mg/L original.

The lower matrix sensitivity explains a low external result under this model. The comparison is not proof of the same mechanism in all future samples.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Extrapolation requires its own justification

The standard-addition line extrapolates to a negative x-intercept near minus 2.008 mg/L in the final flask.Why is this different from reporting an ordinary unknown beyond range?

The negative intercept follows a designed additive model with fixed sample fraction. It is still uncertain and sensitive to model failure. Ordinary high unknowns need new measurements.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: An additive interferent can survive standard addition
text:
An additive interferent can survive standard addition

Blank-corrected response rises with final-flask added analyte; the intercept includes native sample analyte.A positive non-analyte signal can shift the intercept.

Even an excellent straight line can then overestimate native analyte. Background correction must be chemically appropriate.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: Changing final volume changes the design
text:
Changing final volume changes the design

Five flasks have equal sample aliquots and equal final volume, but increasing standard additions expressed as final-flask concentration.Do not use a fixed-volume intercept formula without its fixed-volume conditions.

Different final volumes alter native concentration and matrix fraction. A suitable alternative calculation must account for them.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: Uncertainty belongs to the inferred intercept too
text:
Uncertainty belongs to the inferred intercept too

The standard-addition line extrapolates to a negative x-intercept near minus 2.008 mg/L in the final flask.Slope, intercept, their covariance and volume factors contribute.

This core exercise reports a conditional point estimate. The response interval at zero added analyte is not automatically an interval for original concentration.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: Do not turn one recovery into a universal correction
text:
Do not turn one recovery into a universal correction

Added analyte may not behave like native bound analyte. A successful late spike cannot establish complete extraction of native material.What evidence would support applying a correction to another sample?

Matrix consistency, spike/native equivalence, validated behaviour and correction uncertainty would be needed. A convenient ratio is insufficient.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Transfer the design

Five flasks have equal sample aliquots and equal final volume, but increasing standard additions expressed as final-flask concentration.5.00 mL to 20.00 mL; \(y=0.240+0.120c_{added,final}\).

Negative intercept is minus two mg/L; original concentration is eight mg/L. Require the dilution explanation.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Which method would you trust?

Repeated reference measurements: A is near 10 mg/L, B is tightly grouped near 10.5, and C is spread around 10.The reference is 10.00 mg/L. Compare both location and spread.

Ask for a justification before naming precision or bias. The series are repeat measurements of the same reference material.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Precision concerns repeated results

A and B both have SD about 0.0158 mg/L, while C has SD about 0.316 mg/L.A and B both have SD ≈ 0.0158 mg/L.

Their repeatability is similar. Precision requires stated conditions; repeatability is not the same as all possible between-day or between-laboratory variation.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Bias concerns a suitable reference

Repeated reference measurements: A is near 10 mg/L, B is tightly grouped near 10.5, and C is spread around 10.B mean = 10.50 mg/L: estimated bias +0.50 mg/L.

Reference uncertainty is neglected only in this teaching comparison. A precise series can be displaced.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: A mean close to the reference is not a guarantee
text:
A mean close to the reference is not a guarantee

Repeated reference measurements: A is near 10 mg/L, B is tightly grouped near 10.5, and C is spread around 10.C mean = 10.00 mg/L, but its SD ≈ 0.316 mg/L.

An accidentally close mean in five readings does not validate a method across samples and matrices.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Uncertainty describes doubt under a model
text:
Uncertainty describes doubt under a model
It is not the observed difference from a secretly known true value.

A measurement model relates inputs to the reported quantity. Uncertainty requires relevant input uncertainties and their dependencies.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Retrieve grouped summaries
summarise(n = n(), mean_mg_l = mean(measured_mg_l),
          sd_mg_l = sd(measured_mg_l))

Ask students to interpret the units of SD and variance. SD has the concentration unit; variance has its square.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Spread of readings and uncertainty in a mean differ
text:
Spread of readings and uncertainty in a mean differ
For independent stable readings: \(u_{reading}(\bar x)=s/\sqrt n\).

Name the quantity carefully. This is the reading contribution to the mean, not the SD of future individual readings.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Do not divide shared effects by square root of n
text:
Do not divide shared effects by square root of n

Averaging repeated readings reduces independent reading noise; it does not remove a common stock or preparation effect.A stock error is shared by every reading made from that stock.

Trace the graph from stock through prepared aliquot to repeated readings. Identify which information new readings do and do not add.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
More readings approach a floor

Reading uncertainty decreases with more independent readings, while the combined uncertainty approaches a shared 0.10 mg/L floor.Which curve keeps decreasing? Which levels off?

Solid combines reading uncertainty with a shared 0.10 mg/L component; dashed shows reading alone. These numbers are an independent illustration.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Choose the quantity before choosing the formula
text:
Choose the quantity before choosing the formula

Averaging repeated readings reduces independent reading noise; it does not remove a common stock or preparation effect.One collected sample, several preparations and several readings need different treatment.

The experimental unit comes first. Do not turn dependent data into independent evidence by running a familiar formula.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Write the dilution model

Model: c final = c stock × V aliquot / V final. Result = 10.00 mg/L; input uncertainties are standard uncertainties.\(c=c_sV_a/V_f\).

Inputs: stock one hundred mg/L, aliquot five millilitres, final fifty millilitres. The result is ten mg/L.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Use standard uncertainties of the inputs
text:
Use standard uncertainties of the inputs
Stock: 0.4 mg/L; aliquot: 0.006 mL; final volume: 0.03 mL.

They are supplied standard uncertainties, not tolerance bounds. If only a tolerance is available, a justified distribution model is needed before treating it as standard uncertainty.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Propagate each contribution onto the output scale
text:
Propagate each contribution onto the output scale

Dilution standard uncertainty contributions: stock 0.040, aliquot 0.012 and final volume 0.006 mg/L.Stock contributes 0.040 mg/L.

Use concentration times relative stock uncertainty. All contributions must refer to the reported concentration before combining.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Volume contributions also survive averaging

Dilution standard uncertainty contributions: stock 0.040, aliquot 0.012 and final volume 0.006 mg/L.Aliquot: 0.012 mg/L; final volume: 0.006 mg/L.

Taking additional readings of the prepared flask does not remeasure its actual volume.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Combine independent contributions in quadrature

Dilution standard uncertainty contributions: stock 0.040, aliquot 0.012 and final volume 0.006 mg/L.\(u(c)=\sqrt{0.040^2+0.012^2+0.006^2}\) = 0.04219 mg/L.

The square-root-of-squares rule here assumes independent inputs and a valid first-order approximation. Correlated volumes require covariance terms.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Improve the dominant source first

Dilution standard uncertainty contributions: stock 0.040, aliquot 0.012 and final volume 0.006 mg/L.Would a more precise final flask solve most of this budget?

No: the stock is dominant in this particular example. Do not treat this ranking as universal.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Averaging is useful within its scope
text:
Averaging is useful within its scope

Reading uncertainty decreases with more independent readings, while the combined uncertainty approaches a shared 0.10 mg/L floor.More independent readings reduce the reading component.

Show both curves again and ask where new preparation information would enter. This is not an argument against replication, but for appropriate replication.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
An interval needs a meaning
Standard uncertainty \(u\); expanded uncertainty \(U=ku\); confidence interval for a mean.

Ask which one the previous number represents. It is a standard uncertainty. Do not label every plus/minus quantity as ninety-five percent.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: A small-sample mean uses its sampling model
text:
A small-sample mean uses its sampling model
\(\bar x\pm t_{0.975,n-1}s/\sqrt n\).

This interval assumes independent readings under an appropriate normal model. It does not supply sampling or recovery uncertainty missing from the measurement design.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Treat a known bias as a problem to investigate
text:
Treat a known bias as a problem to investigate

Repeated reference measurements: A is near 10 mg/L, B is tightly grouped near 10.5, and C is spread around 10.An arbitrary error bar does not correct a systematically displaced method.

A justified bias correction has its own uncertainty. Ask which evidence would support correction rather than automatically recentering every dataset.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Report precision that the uncertainty supports
text:
Report precision that the uncertainty supports
10.000 mg/L; standard uncertainty 0.042 mg/L under the stated model.

Retain full numerical precision in code. Round in the report consistently with uncertainty and purpose. State omitted sources.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Transfer: halve the stock uncertainty

Dilution standard uncertainty contributions: stock 0.040, aliquot 0.012 and final volume 0.006 mg/L.Replace 0.4 by 0.2 mg/L. What happens to combined uncertainty?

New standard uncertainty is 0.02408 mg/L, not exactly half of 0.04219 because other components remain.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: What still lies outside the budget?
text:
What still lies outside the budget?

Averaging repeated readings reduces independent reading noise; it does not remove a common stock or preparation effect.Sampling, recovery, matrix effects and unmodelled preparation variation.

Connect this list to the measurand. An uncertainty estimate can be arithmetically correct but incomplete for the decision.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: What relation turns signal into concentration?
text:
What relation turns signal into concentration?

Eighteen iron standards from zero to four mg/L define an absorbance line with a retained intercept.Known final concentrations give measured responses.

State the chemical basis: iron in a matched colour-development assay, response at 510 nm. We will use the chemistry in the UV unit.

title: Calibration and quality control
text:
Fit the measured response direction

Eighteen iron standards from zero to four mg/L define an absorbance line with a retained intercept.\(A=a+bc+e\).

Concentration is set and response is measured with error. Fitting concentration on absorbance is a different least-squares model.

title: Calibration and quality control
text:
Retrieve lm
fit <- lm(absorbance ~ standard_mg_l, data = standards)
coef(fit)

The earlier computing course already used this workflow. Use it to focus on model assumptions rather than reteaching all of R.

title: Calibration and quality control
text:
Interpret the slope with units

Eighteen iron standards from zero to four mg/L define an absorbance line with a retained intercept.Slope ≈ 0.198799 L/mg Fe.

An increase of one mg Fe/L gives about 0.1988 absorbance units in the model. It is not a molar absorptivity without concentration conversion.

title: Calibration and quality control
text:
Retain the estimated intercept

Eighteen iron standards from zero to four mg/L define an absorbance line with a retained intercept.Intercept ≈ 0.003874.

A nonzero offset does not prove a particular cause. Do not force zero or blank-subtract an already blank-referenced response again.

title: Calibration and quality control
text:
Bracket the intended measurement range

Eighteen iron standards from zero to four mg/L define an absorbance line with a retained intercept.These standards cover 0–4 mg Fe/L final.

A good fit here does not establish response at forty mg/L. The range is stated for this teaching scenario, not universally validated.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: Residuals are observations minus fitted responses
text:
Residuals are observations minus fitted responses

Iron calibration residuals scatter around zero without an obvious curved pattern in the selected range.What pattern would challenge a straight line?

Curvature, changing spread or an unusual observation. Ask before revealing the faulty comparison dataset.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: A high R² can hide systematic error
text:
A high R² can hide systematic error

A deliberately curved response leaves systematic patterned residuals after a straight-line fit.The second dataset is deliberately curved.

Even a visually high correlation can leave patterned residuals and biased inverse estimates.

title: Calibration and quality control
text:
Investigate before excluding a standard

A deliberately curved response leaves systematic patterned residuals after a straight-line fit.A point is not wrong merely because it worsens the fit.

Check preparation, transcription, instrument response and protocol. Exclusion needs evidence and a recorded reason.

title: Calibration and quality control
text:
A narrower range needs evidence

A deliberately curved response leaves systematic patterned residuals after a straight-line fit.Which standards and checks would validate the proposed range?

Do not remove upper points solely to improve appearance. Model and range selection must fit the analytical purpose.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: Changing variance is another model concern
text:
Changing variance is another model concern

Iron calibration residuals scatter around zero without an obvious curved pattern in the selected range.Ordinary least squares assumes the specified response-error structure.

If variance grows with concentration, weighting may be appropriate but requires a justified variance model. Recognising the limitation is core; advanced weighted fitting is optional.

title: Calibration and quality control
text:
Invert only after checking applicability

Eighteen iron standards from zero to four mg/L define an absorbance line with a retained intercept.\(\hat c=(\bar A-a)/b\).

For the provided three readings, mean absorbance is 0.480620 and final estimate 2.39813 mg Fe/L. Check range and independent QC before reporting it.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: A concentration estimate is not the original sample result
text:
A concentration estimate is not the original sample result

1.92 × (10/2) × 0.025 = 0.240 mg extracted caffeine; 0.240 / 0.5000 = 0.480 mg/g.The current unit is mg Fe/L in the final coloured solution.

Original concentration needs preparation factors. Ask students which record supplies those factors.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: Three materials ask different QC questions
text:
Three materials ask different QC questions

A blank, independent reference check and a sample spike examine different parts of the measurement.Which would reveal introduced contamination?

A method blank. Then ask which checks calibration under independent known concentration and which probes incremental sample response.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: Independence matters for a check standard
text:
Independence matters for a check standard

A blank, independent reference check and a sample spike examine different parts of the measurement.The same wrong stock can make standards and checks agree.

An independently sourced material can challenge a shared preparation error. Matching matrix and measurand still matter.

title: Calibration and quality control
text:
Acceptance criteria precede the results
What action follows a failure?

Use a documented rule established for the intended procedure. Recalibration, investigation, remeasurement or withholding should follow evidence, not a desire to retain results.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: A weak signal can be detectable but poorly quantified
text:
A weak signal can be detectable but poorly quantified

Twelve independent blank responses cluster near 0.010; a dashed line marks mean plus three standard deviations.Distinguishing a signal from blanks is a different requirement from precise quantification.

Do not use below-limit as a synonym for zero. Decision probabilities, uncertainty and method conditions matter.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: Estimate blank variation from independent blanks
text:
Estimate blank variation from independent blanks

Twelve independent blank responses cluster near 0.010; a dashed line marks mean plus three standard deviations.Mean = 0.0100; SD = 0.001348 signal units.

The twelve method blanks belong to a separate ideal low-level example. Repeated readings of one blank do not measure all blank-preparation variation.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: Keep a heuristic in its proper role
text:
Keep a heuristic in its proper role

Twelve independent blank responses cluster near 0.010; a dashed line marks mean plus three standard deviations.\(3s_{blank}/b=0.02023\) mg/L; \(10s_{blank}/b=0.06742\) mg/L.

Sensitivity is 0.200 in this separate example. These are illustrative concentration increments, not universally validated LOD and LOQ values.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: A signal threshold includes the blank level
text:
A signal threshold includes the blank level

Twelve independent blank responses cluster near 0.010; a dashed line marks mean plus three standard deviations.Threshold here: mean blank plus three SD.

Do not confuse the response threshold with a blank-relative concentration increment or subtract a blank twice.

title: Calibration and quality control
text:
Uncertainty remains after calibration inversion

Averaging repeated readings reduces independent reading noise; it does not remove a common stock or preparation effect.Reading noise and uncertain slope/intercept both contribute.

Use the supplied inverse helper, which propagates coefficient covariance. A forward response prediction interval is not a concentration interval.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: Use the supplied helper with its assumptions
text:
Use the supplied helper with its assumptions
source("R/inverse-calibration.R")
inverse_calibration(fit, unknown_absorbance)

Independent normal equal-variance response errors, known standard concentrations and a well-determined positive slope. First-order approximation; not a general nonlinear/weighted inverse solver.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: Interpret the interval on the correct scale
text:
Interpret the interval on the correct scale
Final concentration ≈ 2.3981 mg Fe/L; approximate 95% interval 2.3886–2.4077.

The interval excludes sample preparation, volumes, sampling and matrix/recovery bias. Ask what must be added before interpreting it as a complete original-sample uncertainty.

text:
Transfer: decide on three failures

A blank, independent reference check and a sample spike examine different parts of the measurement.Outside range; failed independent check; below quantification requirement.

Outside range needs appropriate new measurement; failed check requires investigation and withheld affected results; weak response needs an appropriate qualified report rather than a manufactured zero.

title: UV and visible absorption
text:
The analytical question
How much dissolved iron is in the supplied filtered water, and which results are supported by the measurements? We will make a coloured iron complex, use its light absorption to estimate concentration, then check the preparation factor, calibration, and independent quality-control result.
Use your familiar R project, CSV, plotting, and straight-line skills. The new steps are matching preparation records by ID and accounting for uncertainty when converting a signal to concentration.
Download the complete project, extract it, and open analyticalchem.Rproj. Keep report.Rmd at the project root. The project needs R packages readr, dplyr, ggplot2, knitr, and rmarkdown. If required, install them once in the R console:

install.packages(c("readr", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "knitr", "rmarkdown"))

All measurements here are simulated. This is an analysis exercise; use an approved practical protocol for any actual laboratory work.

title: UV and visible absorption
section: Make an absorber we can measure
text:
Make an absorber we can measure
Iron(II) reacts with 1,10-phenanthroline, abbreviated phen, to form a red-orange complex:
\[\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + 3\,phen \rightleftharpoons [Fe(phen)_3]^{2+}}\]
Three bidentate ligands coordinate one iron ion. We measure the complex near 510 nm. Reduction maintains the iron(II) state; controlled acidity and excess ligand support colour formation. University laboratory background



One Fe²⁺ combines with three phen ligands. Boxes describe stoichiometry, not molecular geometry.


For this exercise, assume quantitative reduction and complex formation and no iron loss. The measurand is mg Fe/L in the supplied filtered water, including iron converted to Fe(II) in the assumed preparation. It is not the original Fe(II) concentration before treatment. No evidence about particulate iron or digestion recovery is supplied.
Predict: if reduction is incomplete, will the result be biased high or low? Explain using the species that absorbs the light.

title: UV and visible absorption
text:
Connect the apparatus to absorbance
At a selected wavelength, light passes through a cuvette. The detector measures transmitted intensity \(I\) relative to reference intensity \(I_0\):
\[T = I/I_0, \qquad A = -\log_{10}(T)\]
A reagent blank contains the preparation reagents without the analyte and accounts for their background under matched conditions. Absorbance in these files is already referenced to a reagent blank. Do not blank-correct it again.



Selected light crosses a 1.00 cm path; the detector measures transmitted light.


A transmittance of 0.50 corresponds to absorbance 0.301. If twice as much analyte doubles absorbance within the linear range, it does not halve transmittance: \(T=10^{-A}\).
For an appropriate dilute solution at fixed wavelength and path length, Beer–Lambert behaviour is \(A=\varepsilon l c\), with \(c\) in mol/L when using a molar absorptivity. Here our calibration uses mg of elemental Fe/L, so its slope has units L/mg Fe. Do not substitute that slope into a molar equation without converting the concentration basis.

title: UV and visible absorption
section: Choose the wavelength from a spectrum
text:
Choose the wavelength from a spectrum

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
spectra <- read_csv("data/spectra.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ggplot(spectra, aes(wavelength_nm, absorbance, colour = trace)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Wavelength (nm)", y = "Absorbance", colour = "Solution") +
  theme_minimal()




The illustrative standard has a maximum near 510 nm; the reagent blank is small.


The spectral shape supports choosing 510 nm for a strong response. A maximum also makes a small wavelength-setting error less consequential than on a steep spectral flank. It does not prove that other sample components cannot absorb. This simulated envelope is not a reference spectrum for identifying a compound.
Each row is a wavelength in one scan. These rows do not give hundreds of independently prepared standards.

title: UV and visible absorption
text:
Fit the familiar calibration

standards <- read_csv("data/standards.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fit <- lm(absorbance ~ standard_mg_l, data = standards)
coef(fit)
a <- unname(coef(fit)[1])
b <- unname(coef(fit)[2])
ggplot(standards, aes(standard_mg_l, absorbance)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(intercept = a, slope = b) +
  labs(x = "Iron in final solution (mg Fe/L)",
       y = "Absorbance at 510 nm") +
  theme_minimal()




Eighteen simulated calibration solutions cover 0–4 mg Fe/L.


The fitted relationship is approximately \(A=0.003874+0.198799c\). The nonzero intercept is estimated, not forced to zero. Its existence alone does not identify the source of the offset.
The concentration is deliberately set; absorbance is the response. Fitting standard_mg_l ~ absorbance describes a different regression. Estimate an unknown using the inverse of our fitted response model:
\[\hat c_{final} = (\bar A_{unknown}-a)/b\]

standards <- standards |> mutate(residual = residuals(fit))
ggplot(standards, aes(standard_mg_l, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Iron in final solution (mg Fe/L)",
       y = "Observed minus fitted absorbance") +
  theme_minimal()




Residuals reveal departures from the line, not whether the sample matrix is compatible.


Look for curvature, changing spread, and unusual observations. Small residuals on standards cannot establish recovery or selectivity in an unknown water. Do not remove a point simply to improve the fit.

title: UV and visible absorption
section: Match the measurement to its preparation
text:
Match the measurement to its preparation
P01 and P02 are separate preparations of W1, each read three times. We will first analyse P01. P03 and P04 belong to W2; P04 is a newly measured preparation with a smaller aliquot. P05 belongs to a later measurement block.



W1 is one supplied water sample with two preparations and three readings per preparation.



readings <- read_csv("data/readings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
preparations <- read_csv("data/preparations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(preparations$preparation_id),
          all(readings$preparation_id %in% preparations$preparation_id))
means <- readings |>
  group_by(preparation_id) |>
  summarise(m = n(), mean_absorbance = mean(absorbance),
            .groups = "drop")
joined <- means |> left_join(preparations, by = "preparation_id")
joined

left_join() attaches the matching preparation information to each measurement summary using the ID. It does not assume that the files have the same row order. The checks require one preparation record per key and a match for every measured preparation. Inspect IDs, row count, units, and missing values after joining.
For P01, mean absorbance is 0.480620, corresponding to about 2.398 mg Fe/L in the final coloured solution.

title: UV and visible absorption
section: Return to the original water concentration
text:
Return to the original water concentration



A 10.00 mL aliquot is made up to 50.00 mL total, including all reagents and solvent.


\[\hat c_{original}=\hat c_{final}\frac{V_{final}}{V_{aliquot}}\]
For P01, \(V_{final}=50.00\) mL and \(V_{aliquot}=10.00\) mL. Multiply by 5, giving about 11.99 mg Fe/L in the supplied water. The final volume is the total volume, not the amount of water added.
Predict: P04 uses 5.00 mL made up to 50.00 mL. Should its final concentration be multiplied by 5 or 10? Which recorded field tells you?

title: UV and visible absorption
section: Check range before reporting a number
text:
Check range before reporting a number
For this exercise, require every repeated reading to lie between the fitted responses at the lowest and highest calibration concentrations. This is a supplied working-range rule, not a general validation of the method.

response_limits <- predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(standard_mg_l = c(0, 4)))
range_check <- readings |>
  group_by(preparation_id) |>
  summarise(in_range = all(absorbance >= response_limits[1] &
                          absorbance <= response_limits[2]), .groups = "drop")
range_check




P03 exceeds the calibrated response range; P04 is a newly measured dilution within range.


P03 is outside range. Its old signal cannot be rescued by changing a dilution factor in the table. P04 is a new measurement of a new aliquot: its mean absorbance is 0.540610 and its dilution factor is 10. This gives about 27.00 mg Fe/L for W2 under the stated assumptions.

title: UV and visible absorption
text:
Use an independent quality-control check
An independently sourced check solution contains 2.00 mg Fe/L in the final solution. Our exercise acceptance window is 95–105% recovery. It checks the calibration in block A and again before the later block B.

qc <- read_csv("data/qc.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
qc_summary <- qc |>
  group_by(block) |>
  summarise(mean_absorbance = mean(absorbance),
            reference_mg_l = first(reference_mg_l), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(estimated_mg_l = (mean_absorbance - a) / b,
         recovery_percent = 100 * estimated_mg_l / reference_mg_l,
         qc_pass = recovery_percent >= 95 & recovery_percent <= 105)
qc_summary




Block A passes the exercise QC rule; the later block B fails.


A recovers about 99.6%. B recovers about 85.2%. Withhold P05 from B, even though its signal is inside the calibration range. Investigate, correct the problem, establish satisfactory calibration and QC, and remeasure the sample. Do not automatically divide results by 0.852: the cause of the failure is not established. A passing simple check also does not prove that every sample matrix is free from interference.
Now combine the two checks so unsupported estimates cannot appear as results:

results <- joined |>
  left_join(range_check, by = "preparation_id") |>
  left_join(qc_summary |> select(block, qc_pass), by = "block") |>
  mutate(reportable = in_range & qc_pass,
         final_mg_l = if_else(reportable,
                              (mean_absorbance - a) / b, NA_real_),
         original_mg_l = final_mg_l * final_ml / aliquot_ml)
results |> select(preparation_id, sample_id, original_mg_l, reportable)
write_csv(results, "output/student-concentrations.csv", na = "NA")

Missing values here mean withheld analytical estimates, not zero iron. Include the reason for withholding in your report.

title: UV and visible absorption
section: Extend the earlier course with uncertainty
text:
Extend the earlier course with uncertainty
Repeated readings do not remove uncertainty in the calibration or in the preparation volumes. A simple concentration estimate also needs uncertainty from the fitted slope and intercept. NIST calibration guidance
Run the supplied helper for P01; you do not need to write a function:

source("R/inverse-calibration.R")
p01_readings <- readings |> filter(preparation_id == "P01")
u_p01 <- inverse_calibration(fit, p01_readings$absorbance)
u_p01

It returns the point estimate, an approximate standard uncertainty from response and calibration, and an approximate 95% interval for final concentration. For P01, these are about 2.3981 mg Fe/L, 0.00451 mg Fe/L, and 2.3886–2.4077 mg Fe/L respectively. These are different summaries: standard uncertainty is not a 95% half-width.
The helper assumes a correct linear model, independent normal response errors with constant variance, negligible calibration-concentration uncertainty, and the same reading variance for standards and unknowns. It uses a first-order approximation appropriate for this well-determined slope. It does not validate those assumptions for another dataset. Forward predict() intervals alone are not concentration intervals; the helper propagates through the inverse relation.
Add independent supplied volume uncertainties using the relation below. Here \(u\) denotes standard uncertainty:
\[u(c_{original})=\sqrt{(D u(c_{final}))^2+
\left(c_{original}\frac{u(V_{final})}{V_{final}}\right)^2+
\left(c_{original}\frac{u(V_{aliquot})}{V_{aliquot}}\right)^2}\]

p01 <- results |> filter(preparation_id == "P01")
D <- p01$final_ml / p01$aliquot_ml
u_original <- sqrt(
  (D * u_p01$u_cal_mg_l)^2 +
  (p01$original_mg_l * p01$u_final_ml / p01$final_ml)^2 +
  (p01$original_mg_l * p01$u_aliquot_ml / p01$aliquot_ml)^2)
u_original




Response and calibration dominate this illustrative uncertainty budget for P01.


One suitable statement is: P01 gave 11.991 mg Fe/L with a standard uncertainty of 0.028 mg Fe/L from the stated calibration, reading, and volume model. This is not a full method uncertainty or a 95% interval. The budget excludes sampling, matrix bias, incomplete recovery, and uncertain standard concentrations. Keep full precision for calculations and round only reported values.
P01 and P02 share a calibration and come from the same collected sample. Do not average their uncertainty estimates as though they were independent calibrations, or describe six readings as six water samples.

title: UV and visible absorption
text:
Your report and transfer task

Render the supplied report.Rmd unchanged, then save an edited copy at the project root. Explain the absorber, wavelength, concentration basis, and assumed preparation chemistry.
Add the spectral, calibration, and residual plots with your interpretations.
Complete the ID join, range checks, and QC checks. Report P01, P02, and P04 separately and explain why P03 and P05 do not have reportable concentrations.
Add P01’s uncertainty calculation and state the omissions. Explain why the SD of its three absorbances alone is insufficient.
For a new preparation, a 2.00 mL aliquot was made up to 50.00 mL. Its three readings are 0.399, 0.401, and 0.400 in accepted block A. Estimate the original concentration. Compare its preparation factor with P01’s.
Restart R and render using rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports") from the console. Keep the source, input data, CSV results, and HTML report together.







Numerical checks





P01 ≈ 11.99 mg Fe/L, P02 ≈ 12.10 mg Fe/L, P04 ≈ 27.00 mg Fe/L. P03 needs remeasurement; P05 is withheld after QC failure. For the new preparation, \(\bar A=0.400\), \(D=25\), and the original concentration is approximately 49.81 mg Fe/L. This is a point estimate, not a complete uncertainty statement.









Check your reasoning






Incomplete reduction? Less absorbing Fe(II) complex can give a low result.
Why not subtract the blank again? The supplied absorbances already use it as the reference. A further subtraction would change the measurement basis.
Why is a good line insufficient? Sample range, recovery, selectivity, preparation, and current QC still matter.
Does a QC failure identify its cause? No. It signals that results need to be withheld and the measurement process investigated.
Can more scans replace more samples? No. Wavelength positions and repeated readings are not independently collected waters.

title: Separation principles
section: A mixture becomes a sequence of signals
text:
A mixture becomes a sequence of signals
A detector can respond to more than one component. Chromatography changes when components reach it, allowing their responses to be distinguished if the separation is adequate. You will connect phase exchange with retention, calculate retention factors and resolution, and explain why an integrated area may cease to be analyte-specific when peaks overlap.



Different bands occupy different positions inside a column before they reach the detector.


This is a snapshot inside the column. A chromatogram is a detector response over time at its outlet. The less retained band reaches the outlet earlier; the more retained band spends a larger fraction of time in the stationary phase. The bands also spread during migration, so different mean retention times alone do not guarantee useful separation.

title: Separation principles
section: Repeated exchange sets the average speed
text:
Repeated exchange sets the average speed



Solute exchanges between a moving phase and a stationary phase.


The mobile phase carries dissolved or gaseous solute along. Interaction with the stationary phase delays migration. In a simple equilibrium picture the retained amount relative to the amount in mobile phase gives a retention factor. Phase chemistry, temperature and mobile-phase composition can affect that balance. Not every compound has the same selectivity under a given set of conditions.
The unretained marker time \(t_0\) estimates mobile-phase transit. A component’s retention time \(t_R\) includes this transit plus its additional retention:
\[k=\frac{t_R-t_0}{t_0}\]
For \(t_0=1.00\) min and \(t_R=3.00\) min, \(k=2.00\). Using \(t_R/t_0\) instead would give 3 and include the transit time in what is intended to measure extra retention. IUPAC retention factor

title: Separation principles
section: Read a chromatogram with its axes
text:
Read a chromatogram with its axes

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
chrom <- read_csv("data/course/chromatograms.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ggplot(filter(chrom, run == "resolved"), aes(time_min, response)) +
  geom_line() + geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Time (min)", y = "Detector response (arbitrary units)") +
  theme_minimal()




A resolved chromatogram has an unretained marker at one minute and peaks near three and four minutes.


The marker line is not an analyte peak. Retention time can support identity when conditions and a suitable standard agree, but another component can coelute. A chromatogram row is one time position within a run. Hundreds of rows do not mean hundreds of independently sampled materials.
Peak area integrates response over time after an appropriate baseline is established. Peak height is a different quantity. With a fixed amount and response factor, broader peaks can be lower while retaining their area. Neither height nor area is directly concentration until calibrated.

title: Separation principles
section: Calculate resolution using the stated width definition
text:
Calculate resolution using the stated width definition
For baseline widths \(w_1,w_2\) and \(t_{R2}>t_{R1}\),
\[R_s=\frac{2(t_{R2}-t_{R1})}{w_1+w_2}\]
The formula is dimensionless when all times use the same unit. It uses baseline widths. A formula using half-height widths has a different coefficient. Do not substitute a width just because it is available in an export. IUPAC peak resolution

peaks <- read_csv("data/course/peak-summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(k = (t_r_min - t0_min) / t0_min)
resolution <- peaks |>
  group_by(run) |>
  summarise(k_A = k[compound == "A"], k_B = k[compound == "B"],
            alpha = k_B / k_A,
            resolution = 2 * (t_r_min[compound == "B"] -
                               t_r_min[compound == "A"]) /
                          sum(baseline_width_min), .groups = "drop")
resolution
write_csv(resolution, "output/chromatographic-resolution.csv")

The resolved run has \(R_s=2.222\) with \(k_A=2\), \(k_B=3\) and selectivity \(\alpha=1.5\). Values near 1.5 are often used as a useful reference for roughly similar Gaussian peaks, but adequacy depends on shape, relative amount and required quantification accuracy. Do not adopt one threshold as proof of purity.



Changing peak spacing causes overlap despite unchanged component areas.


The overlap run has \(R_s=0.667\). If the detector responds to both components, a combined area does not identify their separate amounts. Drawing a vertical split between maxima is a modelling choice, not new chemical selectivity. Changing separation conditions or using justified additional evidence is preferable to presenting an unsupported single-analyte result.

title: Separation principles
section: Band broadening is another route to lost resolution
text:
Band broadening is another route to lost resolution



Unchanged mean retention times can still produce overlap when the bands broaden.


The broad run has the same retention times as the resolved run but \(R_s=0.909\). Both peak spacing and widths matter. Poor injection conditions, extra-column volume, dispersion and mass-transfer limitations can broaden peaks.
An ideal Gaussian plate estimate uses \(N=16(t_R/w_b)^2\) with baseline width \(w_b\) under its stated assumptions. Higher efficiency means narrower bands for a given retention, but selectivity can be more important than making an already unsuitable separation slightly sharper.



An illustrative plate-height curve balances diffusion and mass-transfer contributions.


The conceptual van Deemter relation \(H=A+B/u+Cu\) explains why very low and very high mobile-phase velocities can both broaden bands through different effects. The plotted values are dimensionless illustrations, not measured optimal settings for an instrument. Real method changes also affect time, pressure, selectivity and sample compatibility.

title: Separation principles
text:
Practical and transfer
Plot the three runs and calculate their retention factors and resolutions. Explain why the lower peak height in the broad run does not automatically mean less analyte. State what evidence would be needed to report a caffeine amount from a peak at the expected retention time in a new beverage matrix.
For a new pair with \(t_0=0.80\) min, \(t_{R1}=2.40\) min, \(t_{R2}=3.20\) min and baseline widths 0.40 and 0.60 min, calculate both retention factors, selectivity and resolution. Which quantities would change if both widths doubled while retention times stayed fixed?






Numerical checks





\(k_1=2.00\), \(k_2=3.00\), \(\alpha=1.50\), and \(R_s=1.60\). Doubling both widths halves \(R_s\) to 0.80 but leaves retention factors and selectivity unchanged. It therefore changes separation adequacy without changing the mean retention order.

title: From sample to answer
section: Start with a question that has a unit
text:
Start with a question that has a unit
A water sample gives a number on an instrument. What does that number represent? Before choosing software, define the measurand: the quantity intended to be measured. Here it is chloride mass concentration, in mg chloride/L, in water collected at a named location and time. The analyte is chloride; the matrix is water and everything else it contains. A response in volts or absorbance is a signal, not yet that chemical quantity.
By the end, you should be able to state a measurand, distinguish concentration from amount, inspect an analytical table in R, and make a restrained comparison of collected samples.



A measurement claim requires a defined sample, quantity, unit and procedure.


“Total iron”, “dissolved iron” and “iron(II)” are different questions. A filter changes the material entering a procedure; a reduction can change oxidation state. A report needs enough preparation information to tell the reader what was actually measured. More decimal places cannot repair an ambiguous question.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Follow the analytical process



Question, sample, prepared solution and recorded signal form a traceable chain.


A useful sequence is: define the question; obtain material that represents it; prepare a known part; obtain a selective enough signal; calibrate and check the measurement; calculate back to the original material; state uncertainty and limitations. R makes the calculations reproducible. It cannot restore analyte lost during storage or establish selectivity from a spreadsheet column name.
A qualitative question asks whether evidence supports the presence or identity of a substance. A quantitative question asks how much. A matching retention time is evidence of identity under the stated conditions, but another compound can share it. Quantification requires the intended analyte to account for the measured response well enough for the question.



Conductivity and a chloride-selective procedure respond to different properties of the same water.


For example, conductivity responds to several mobile ionic species. A low conductivity reading is not automatically a low chloride concentration. Choose a procedure whose response can be related to the proposed measurand.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Retrieve the R workflow
Download the course project from the link below, extract it, and open analyticalchem.Rproj. Run R in the R console. Files in data/ are untouched inputs; save derived results in output/. All datasets in this course are simulated teaching data. Read data/course/README.md for their chemical assumptions and column definitions.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
water <- read_csv("data/course/water.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(water)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(water$sample_id),
          all(water$collected_l > 0), !anyNA(water$chloride_mg_l))

One row is one independently collected sample. The four inlet and four outlet samples are not matched pairs. Their row order does not establish a before/after design. Check IDs, units, missing values and the meaning of a row before doing statistics. This supplied table is complete; a missing measurement in another table must not silently become zero.

summary_water <- water |>
  group_by(location) |>
  summarise(n_samples = n(), mean_mg_l = mean(chloride_mg_l),
            sd_mg_l = sd(chloride_mg_l), .groups = "drop")
summary_water

ggplot(water, aes(location, chloride_mg_l)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 7)) +
  labs(x = "Sampling location", y = "Chloride (mg/L)") +
  theme_minimal()




Individual collected samples show the location difference and the spread within each location.


The means are 19.5 and 12.5 mg/L. That is a 7.0 mg/L descriptive difference for these collected samples. The design does not establish a treatment effect or represent every time of day. Start with the individual observations, units, and sampling scope. There is no need to add a hypothesis test to every table.

title: From sample to answer
section: Convert units without changing the quantity
text:
Convert units without changing the quantity
For a homogeneous solution, mass concentration \(c=m/V\), so mass \(m=cV\). A 0.250 L portion at 20.0 mg/L contains 5.00 mg analyte. Taking twice the volume at the same concentration doubles the collected amount, not the concentration.



Five milligrams in a quarter litre corresponds to twenty milligrams per litre.



water <- water |>
  mutate(chloride_g_l = chloride_mg_l / 1000,
         chloride_mg = chloride_mg_l * collected_l)
water |> select(sample_id, chloride_mg_l, chloride_g_l, chloride_mg)
write_csv(water, "output/water-derived.csv")

Keep the unit in the variable name or dictionary, and in every plotted axis. Here 20 mg/L = 0.020 g/L. Converting mg to g without also changing the reported unit would give a thousand-fold error. Do not label every concentration “ppm”: mg/L is a mass-per-volume quantity, whereas a mass fraction needs a mass basis. For dilute water they can sometimes be approximately related using density, but they are not definitions of the same quantity.



Each quarter-litre collected sample contains a calculated amount of chloride.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Practical and transfer
Create course-report.Rmd at the project root from the supplied template. State the measurand and what one row represents. Include the individual-point plot, a location summary with sample counts, one unit conversion, and a paragraph about what the design supports. Save your table and render the report after restarting R.
For a separate unknown, the analysis establishes 0.0750 mg chloride in a 25.00 mL portion. Calculate mg/L. Then state which extra information would be needed to claim a location-wide mean or an uncertainty for the result.






Check your result





\(0.0750/0.02500=3.00\) mg/L. The arithmetic alone supplies neither representative sampling nor an uncertainty estimate. For the supplied water table the inlet mean is 19.5 mg/L and outlet mean 12.5 mg/L; both use four collected samples.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Explain before moving on

Why does filtering a sample matter to the measurand? It changes the material analysed; retained particles do not enter the filtered-water result.
Why plot observations before comparing means? It exposes spread, unusual values and how much evidence supports the summary.
Could a perfectly reproducible report have a wrong result? Yes: a wrong unit, inappropriate method or unrepresentative sample can be reproduced too.
