title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: Why did a plausible result come out low?
text:
Why did a plausible result come out low?
External standards in a simple solvent give one response per unit analyte. The same analyte in a sample matrix can give a different response. A good straight line in the standards does not prove the calibration transfers to the sample. Here you will compare sensitivities, calculate spike recovery, and use a fixed-volume standard-addition model.
The simulated assay measures a dissolved analyte after matched preparation. All signals in this unit are already background corrected. Equal sample aliquots are made to equal final volumes. Those definitions are necessary for the intercept calculation below.



External standards and the sample matrix give different response sensitivities.


A multiplicative matrix effect changes sensitivity. An additive interference contributes signal not proportional to the analyte being added. Standard addition can compensate for some multiplicative effects under suitable conditions. It cannot automatically distinguish native analyte signal from an unrelated additive signal.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: Use a spike to ask a limited question
text:
Use a spike to ask a limited question
Suppose two otherwise matched final solutions contain the same sample fraction. The second includes an extra 1.00 mg/L analyte in its final volume. External calibration estimates 1.50 mg/L for the first and 2.25 mg/L for the second.
\[\mathrm{recovery}(\%)=100\,
\frac{c_{spiked,estimated}-c_{unspiked,estimated}}{c_{added}}\]

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
spikes <- read_csv("data/course/spike-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
recovery_percent <- 100 * diff(spikes$externally_estimated_mg_l_final) /
                          diff(spikes$added_mg_l_final)
recovery_percent




Adding 1.00 mg/L increases the external-calibration estimate by only 0.75 mg/L.


The incremental recovery is 75%. These two records have explicitly ordered unspiked/spiked roles and equal final volume; a general dataset should be matched by its preparation identifiers and roles, not arbitrary row order. No universal acceptance window is assumed here. This result flags a response problem under the example conditions.



A spike before extraction probes different losses from a spike added immediately before injection.


A late spike does not pass through earlier extraction losses. A freely dissolved spike may also differ from native bound analyte. State what the spike tested, when it was added and what chemical equivalence you assume.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: Construct standard additions with fixed sample fraction
text:
Construct standard additions with fixed sample fraction
Each flask receives 10.00 mL of the same sample and is made to 25.00 mL total. Added standard is expressed as mg/L in that final flask. Thus the native sample concentration in every flask is \(c_s(10/25)\).



Equal sample aliquots and equal final volumes keep the sample matrix fraction fixed across additions.


For an additive linear response with sensitivity \(b\) and correctly removed background,
\[y=b\left(c_s\frac{V_s}{V_f}+c_{added,final}\right)\]
Fitting \(y=a+b c_{added,final}\) gives negative x-intercept \(-a/b\). Its magnitude estimates the native concentration after the sample’s dilution into the flask. Recover the original concentration by multiplying by \(V_f/V_s\). IUPAC standard-addition terminology

additions <- read_csv("data/course/standard-addition.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fit_sa <- lm(blank_corrected_signal ~ spike_mg_l_final, data = additions)
a_sa <- unname(coef(fit_sa)[1])
b_sa <- unname(coef(fit_sa)[2])
x_intercept <- -a_sa / b_sa
original_mg_l <- -x_intercept * 25.00 / 10.00
c(x_intercept_mg_l_final = x_intercept, original_mg_l = original_mg_l)




Measured additions give a line whose intercept depends on the native analyte already present.


The fitted intercept is 0.3004, slope 0.1496, and x-intercept about −2.0080 mg/L. The original concentration is therefore 5.020 mg/L. It is a conditional point estimate; neither the intercept nor the dilution volumes are exact.



The negative intercept is a model-based extrapolation specific to the standard-addition design.


We do not physically prepare negative analyte. Extrapolation is justified only through this specified signal model and design. Curvature, changing matrix fraction, poor background correction or different behaviour of added and native analyte can invalidate it. Ordinary unknowns beyond an external-calibration range still need new measurements; this design is a different inference problem.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Compare the external-calibration answer

external <- read_csv("data/course/external-matrix.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fit_ext <- lm(blank_corrected_signal ~ c_mg_l, data = external)
external_final <- (additions$blank_corrected_signal[1] - coef(fit_ext)[1]) /
                    coef(fit_ext)[2]
external_original <- unname(external_final) * 25 / 10
external_original
write_csv(data.frame(standard_addition_mg_l = original_mg_l,
                     external_calibration_mg_l = external_original,
                     incremental_spike_recovery_percent = recovery_percent),
          "output/matrix-comparison.csv")

The external estimate is about 3.761 mg/L. The lower matrix sensitivity explains its low result under the simulation model. This is not a reason to divide every unknown by a single recovery factor: samples can have different matrices, and an observed failure need not have the assumed cause.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Practical and transfer
Report both calibration answers, the spike calculation, standard-addition plot, negative-intercept interpretation and dilution correction. Explain why the background assumption matters and list one failure that standard addition would not solve. For this introductory unit, retain the point-estimate status and identify the uncertain intercept/slope and volumes; do not call the fitted intercept’s response interval a concentration interval.
For a new fixed-volume design, 5.00 mL sample is made to 20.00 mL total in every flask. The line is \(y=0.240+0.120 c_{added,final}\). Calculate the original concentration. What if all flasks instead received different final volumes without a volume correction?






Numerical and design checks





\(x_0=-2.00\) mg/L; original concentration is 8.00 mg/L. Different final volumes change native concentration and matrix fraction, so the simple fixed-volume intercept formula no longer applies directly.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Reproducible is not necessarily close to the reference
text:
Reproducible is not necessarily close to the reference
Three methods repeatedly measure the same reference material at 10.00 mg/L. You will compare their bias and spread, then propagate uncertainty through a dilution. The goal is to explain what improves when readings are repeated and what remains shared by all readings.
Precision concerns closeness among repeated measurements under specified conditions. Bias is a systematic departure estimated against a suitable reference. Measurement uncertainty expresses doubt about a result under its measurement model. It is not the difference from a secretly known true value. An uncertainty budget needs the relevant sources, including sources not visible in a short set of repeat readings.



Method B is precise but displaced from the reference; method C is more dispersed.



library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
measurements <- read_csv("data/course/precision.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
summary_precision <- measurements |>
  group_by(method) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_mg_l = mean(measured_mg_l),
            sd_mg_l = sd(measured_mg_l),
            u_mean_mg_l = sd_mg_l / sqrt(n),
            bias_mg_l = mean_mg_l - first(reference_mg_l),
            .groups = "drop")
summary_precision

A and B both have SD about 0.0158 mg/L, but B’s mean is 10.50 mg/L: its estimated bias is +0.50 mg/L. C has mean 10.00 mg/L but SD about 0.316 mg/L. A mean close to the reference in one small series does not prove the method is unbiased in all matrices. Here reference uncertainty is neglected for the comparison; real bias evaluation must include it.



The same small SD for A and B does not reveal B’s bias.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Which uncertainty does dividing by square root of n estimate?
text:
Which uncertainty does dividing by square root of n estimate?
For independent readings of one stable prepared solution, \(s/\sqrt n\) estimates the reading contribution to uncertainty in their mean. It does not describe the spread among future individual readings, nor does it reduce a shared standard-concentration error or lost analyte. Independence and the quantity being averaged matter more than the availability of sqrt().



Stock concentration and preparation effects are shared by repeat readings.


If reading uncertainty is \(0.20/\sqrt n\) mg/L and another independent shared component is 0.10 mg/L, the combined standard uncertainty is \(\sqrt{0.20^2/n+0.10^2}\). More readings approach a floor of 0.10 mg/L, not zero. This is an illustrative model; the numbers are not estimated from the earlier reference-material table.



Repeating readings reduces the dashed reading contribution but not the shared component in the solid curve.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Propagate a transparent dilution model
A stock concentration is 100.0 mg/L with standard uncertainty 0.4 mg/L. A 5.000 mL aliquot has standard uncertainty 0.006 mL; final volume 50.00 mL has standard uncertainty 0.03 mL. Treat the three inputs as independent for this example. The model is \(c=c_sV_a/V_f\), giving 10.00 mg/L.
For small independent uncertainties, add squared contributions:
\[u(c)=c\sqrt{\left(\frac{u(c_s)}{c_s}\right)^2+
\left(\frac{u(V_a)}{V_a}\right)^2+
\left(\frac{u(V_f)}{V_f}\right)^2}\]
The sign of a derivative matters when covariances are present; in this independent example its squared contribution is positive. Two volumes from a shared calibration or common temperature effect need not be independent. The formula is conditional on the model, not a licence to ignore correlations.

c_stock <- 100
u_stock <- 0.4
v_aliquot <- 5
u_aliquot <- 0.006
v_final <- 50
u_final <- 0.03
c_final <- c_stock * v_aliquot / v_final
contributions <- c(stock = c_final * u_stock / c_stock,
                   aliquot = c_final * u_aliquot / v_aliquot,
                   final = c_final * u_final / v_final)
u_c <- sqrt(sum(contributions^2))
c(concentration_mg_l = c_final, standard_uncertainty_mg_l = u_c)




The stock concentration dominates this particular dilution budget.


The contributions are 0.040, 0.012 and 0.006 mg/L. Combined \(u(c)=0.04219\) mg/L. If improvement is needed, reducing the dominant stock uncertainty is more promising than taking more readings of the already prepared solution. Eurachem uncertainty guidance

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
State what your interval means
A standard uncertainty is expressed on an SD-like scale. An expanded uncertainty is \(U=ku\) with a stated coverage factor and justification. A confidence interval for an estimated mean is another construction, using its sampling model. Do not call every “±” number a 95% interval.
For a normal mean based on independent readings, an appropriate t interval uses \(\bar x\pm t_{0.975,n-1}s/\sqrt n\). For the small dilution budget above, simply multiplying by 2 may be a useful approximate expanded uncertainty under further conditions, but those conditions and the intended coverage must be stated. A known significant bias is investigated or corrected with appropriate uncertainty; adding an arbitrary error bar does not correct it.
Keep unrounded quantities in code. A concise reported dilution result could be 10.000 mg/L with standard uncertainty 0.042 mg/L under the stated independent- input model. The reporting precision should match the uncertainty and purpose, not the maximum digits printed by R.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Practical and transfer
Save the method summaries, dilution inputs and uncertainty contributions in output/. Report one example of good repeatability with bias, and explain why the dilution model is incomplete for an extracted environmental sample.

write_csv(summary_precision, "output/precision-summary.csv")
write_csv(data.frame(source = names(contributions),
                     u_mg_l = as.numeric(contributions)),
          "output/dilution-budget.csv")

For a new stock with the same concentration but standard uncertainty 0.2 mg/L, recompute the combined uncertainty. Separately, calculate C’s uncertainty in its mean from its five readings. Explain why the two answers describe different measurement processes.






Numerical checks





The improved stock gives \(u(c)=\sqrt{0.020^2+0.012^2+0.006^2}\) = 0.02408 mg/L. Method C’s reading contribution is 0.1414 mg/L. Neither number incorporates sampling, matrix recovery or an unknown common bias.



Ask yourself: what quantity has SD 0.316 mg/L, what quantity has uncertainty 0.141 mg/L, and which effect would remain after infinitely many readings?

title: Calibration and quality control
section: Can this response support a concentration?
text:
Can this response support a concentration?
A calibration relates known analyte quantities to measured responses. You will retrieve the straight-line fit from introductory computing, inspect whether its assumptions suit the data, and distinguish working range, blank response and independent checks. We reuse the iron standards later measured in the UV/visible unit: concentrations refer to mg elemental Fe/L in the final coloured solution; absorbance is already reagent-blank referenced.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: Fit the response model in the measured direction
text:
Fit the response model in the measured direction

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
standards <- read_csv("data/standards.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fit <- lm(absorbance ~ standard_mg_l, data = standards)
a <- unname(coef(fit)[1])
b <- unname(coef(fit)[2])
coef(fit)




Known final concentrations and independently prepared standard responses define a fitted line.


We set concentration and observe absorbance. The model is \(A=a+bc+e\), with response error \(e\). Its least-squares fit gives \(a\approx0.003874\) and \(b\approx0.198799\) L/mg Fe. The fitted offset is retained. A near-zero concentration does not force a precisely zero measured response.
Calibration standards should bracket the intended measurements. Use an independently sourced check where possible: if every standard and check comes from the same wrongly assigned stock, their agreement can conceal the problem.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: Look at the residuals, not just a summary statistic
text:
Look at the residuals, not just a summary statistic

standards <- standards |>
  mutate(fitted = fitted(fit), residual = residuals(fit))
ggplot(standards, aes(standard_mg_l, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Final iron concentration (mg Fe/L)", y = "Residual absorbance") +
  theme_minimal()




Residuals in the selected range have no obvious curved pattern.


A large \(R^2\) can coexist with systematic curvature. Residuals should be assessed against concentration or fitted response, looking for curvature, changing spread or an unusual observation. Investigate records and measurement conditions before excluding a point. If response variance changes strongly with concentration, ordinary unweighted fitting may be inappropriate; recognise that limitation rather than automatically adopting a more complicated model.



A second deliberately curved dataset leaves patterned residuals after a straight-line fit.


In nonlinear-calibration.csv, the curve is an intentional teaching fault. One option is a justified narrower range with adequate standards; another is a validated alternative model. Deleting high standards simply to obtain a prettier line is not validation. Keep model choice and working-range evidence explicit.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: Invert the line, then check its applicability
text:
Invert the line, then check its applicability
For a mean unknown absorbance, \(\hat c=(\bar A-a)/b\). This is an inverse estimate from a model of response. Reversing the regression to c ~ A is a different least-squares problem and is not the same calculation.

unknown_absorbance <- c(0.47922, 0.48041, 0.48223)
response_limits <- predict(fit,
  newdata = data.frame(standard_mg_l = c(0, 4)))
in_range <- all(unknown_absorbance >= response_limits[1] &
                unknown_absorbance <= response_limits[2])
unknown_mg_l <- if (in_range) (mean(unknown_absorbance) - a) / b else NA_real_
unknown_mg_l

The result is about 2.398 mg Fe/L in the final solution. It says nothing about the original sample concentration until its preparation factors are applied. Passing this range rule does not establish selectivity in a different sample matrix.

title: Calibration and quality control
text:
Three quality-control questions



A blank, independent check and sample spike diagnose different aspects of the process.


A method blank goes through the preparation without the sample and detects introduced contamination or background. A reagent blank used as the optical reference and a whole-procedure method blank are not always the same material. An independent check challenges calibration accuracy under the check’s conditions. A sample spike probes response to added analyte in that matrix and from its point of addition onward. State preselected acceptance criteria and what happens when a check fails; do not invent a criterion after viewing results.

title: Calibration and quality control
text:
Detection is not reliable quantification
A weak signal can be distinguishable from blanks while still having unacceptable relative uncertainty for quantification. Detection and quantification limits depend on the procedure, noise model, decision probabilities and performance requirements. The following is only an indicative teaching calculation in a separate ideal response model with sensitivity 0.200 signal units per mg/L.

blanks <- read_csv("data/course/blank-signals.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
s_blank <- sd(blanks$signal)
indicative <- data.frame(
  blank_mean = mean(blanks$signal), blank_sd = s_blank,
  detection_mg_l = 3 * s_blank / 0.200,
  quantification_mg_l = 10 * s_blank / 0.200)
indicative




The illustrative mean-plus-three-SD signal threshold is shown against independent blank responses.


The blank mean is 0.0100 and SD 0.001348 signal units. The corresponding rough 3-SD and 10-SD concentration increments are 0.02023 and 0.06742 mg/L. The signal threshold includes the blank mean; these concentration increments are relative to that blank, not a second correction to the iron dataset. These multipliers are not universal validation criteria. A below-limit result is not evidence of exactly zero analyte.

title: Calibration and quality control
text:
Include uncertainty in inverse estimation

source("R/inverse-calibration.R")
unknown_uncertainty <- inverse_calibration(fit, unknown_absorbance)
unknown_uncertainty
write_csv(unknown_uncertainty, "output/calibration-unknown.csv")

The supplied helper includes reading noise and the slope/intercept covariance in a first-order inverse calculation. It assumes a correct linear model, independent normal constant-variance response errors, negligible uncertainty in standard concentrations, and a well-determined positive slope. Its approximate 95% interval is about 2.3886–2.4077 mg Fe/L, before preparation uncertainty. A forward response prediction interval is not itself a concentration interval. NIST inverse-calibration guidance

title: Calibration and quality control
text:
Practical and transfer
Report the line with units, residual interpretation, unknown concentration and its conditional interval. Write decisions for (a) a sample beyond range, (b) a failed independent check, and (c) a weak response below an established quantification limit. For the curved dataset, make the residual plot and explain what additional evidence a proposed narrower range would need.
As a transfer calculation, a signal SD of 0.004 and sensitivity 0.500 give which rough 3-SD concentration increment? Would doubling the number of readings of one blank establish the whole method’s detection performance?






Check the calculation and scope





\(3(0.004)/0.500=0.024\) mg/L. Reading one blank more often does not assess between-preparation blank variation, contamination or performance in real samples. More repeat readings and more independent method blanks are different designs.

Attach a preparation by ID

  left_join(preparations, by = "preparation_id")

Fit a line and respect its direction
fit <- lm(response ~ known_concentration, data = standards)
coef(fit)
residuals(fit)
The response is on the left. An inverse concentration estimate uses the fitted response relationship; fitting the variables in the opposite direction is a different regression. Inspect residuals, range and QC before exporting results.

title: R reference for analytical measurements

Logarithms and differences

log10(0.0001)
10^(-4)
diff(c(0, 1, 1.5, 2))

log10() gives a base-ten logarithm; 10^x reverses it. The logarithm of a physical quantity is taken relative to a stated reference/unit convention. diff() gives consecutive differences. A titration derivative divides the pH differences by the corresponding volume differences, not by the number of rows.

title: Atomic measurements
section: Measure an element rather than its original molecule
text:
Measure an element rather than its original molecule
An elemental method can report copper in plant material after an appropriate preparation. It does not preserve the original molecules or prove which oxidation state the copper had. You will compare atomic absorption and emission, then calculate copper per dry sample mass from a digest and a further dilution.



Absorption raises atomic energy using incident light; emission releases light from an excited population.


In atomic absorption, an element-specific source provides light absorbed by free atoms. In optical emission, an excited population emits photons at characteristic wavelengths. Both require suitable sample introduction and control of interferences. Absorption and emission are not simply two names for the coloured-solution method: atomisation changes the sample substantially.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Follow each instrument’s signal path



AAS compares source light transmitted through a population of free atoms.


A flame supplies a continuously introduced atom population. A graphite furnace uses a small aliquot and a heating program with drying, matrix removal and atomisation stages. The useful response and interferences depend on those conditions. Small sample volume alone does not determine fitness for purpose.



ICP optical emission introduces an aerosol into a plasma and separates the emitted wavelengths.


ICP-OES uses plasma excitation and a spectrometer to distinguish emission wavelengths. Multi-element measurement is possible, but line choice, background, transport effects and spectral overlap still need attention. Manufacturer description of the ICP-OES signal path



Flame, furnace and plasma approaches differ in introduction and atomisation conditions.


The cheapest or most sensitive instrument is not automatically the best choice. Consider required range, matrix, available sample amount, number of elements, throughput and preparation. ICP-MS would detect ions by mass-to-charge rather than the emitted optical signal; do not confuse it with ICP-OES.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Spectral selectivity has limits
A neighbouring element line or structured background can contribute near a selected wavelength. An apparently stable signal can still be biased. Examine a suitable spectral window, alternative lines or an appropriate interference correction under the method, rather than attributing every count to copper.



An illustrative neighbouring line alters the spectrum around the target emission.


These profiles are simulated illustrations near 324.75 nm, not identification reference spectra. A real line assignment and correction require validated wavelength and instrument information. Chemical and transport effects can also change the atom population without producing a visibly separate optical peak.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Calibrate the measured solution
The supplied standards describe copper in the solution introduced for emission measurement, in mg/L. The sample data include an independently processed method blank and independent QC materials. All counts are raw on the exercise’s instrument response scale; the fitted intercept is retained.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
standards <- read_csv("data/course/atomic-standards.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fit <- lm(emission_counts ~ copper_mg_l, data = standards)
a <- unname(coef(fit)[1])
b <- unname(coef(fit)[2])
qc <- read_csv("data/course/atomic-qc.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(estimated_mg_l = (emission_counts - a) / b,
         recovery_percent = 100 * estimated_mg_l / reference_mg_l,
         qc_pass = recovery_percent >= recovery_lower &
                   recovery_percent <= recovery_upper)
qc




The calibration describes copper in the introduced solution, not directly in the dry plant.





Both independent checks pass the supplied 95–105% exercise window.


A passing dissolved check tests response under its conditions. It does not prove complete digestion of plant material. The plant result below is conditional on quantitative transfer/recovery; a suitable reference material or recovery study would be needed to establish that assumption for real samples.

title: Atomic measurements
section: Reverse dilution, then subtract the correct blank basis
text:
Reverse dilution, then subtract the correct blank basis
A1 begins with 0.2500 g dry material made to 50.00 mL digest. A further twofold dilution is measured. The method blank is a separately processed digest measured without that further dilution. First convert both signals to concentration; undo the sample’s further dilution; then subtract the method blank on the digest concentration basis.

digests <- read_csv("data/course/atomic-digests.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
blank_digest_mg_l <- (digests$emission_counts[digests$sample_id == "method_blank"] - a) / b
results <- digests |>
  mutate(measured_mg_l = (emission_counts - a) / b,
         in_range = measured_mg_l >= 0 & measured_mg_l <= 2,
         digest_corrected_mg_l = measured_mg_l * further_dilution -
                                  blank_digest_mg_l,
         copper_mg_kg = if_else(sample_id != "method_blank" & in_range &
                                 all(qc$qc_pass),
           digest_corrected_mg_l * (digest_ml / 1000) / (dry_mass_g / 1000),
           NA_real_))
results
write_csv(results, "output/copper-dry-mass.csv", na = "NA")

A1’s measured concentration is about 0.40189 mg/L; digest concentration after undoing dilution and subtracting the blank is 0.80179 mg/L. The digest contains 0.04009 mg Cu. Divide by 0.0002500 kg dry material to obtain 160.36 mg/kg dry mass. The method blank has no dry sample mass and no mg/kg sample result.



Derived plant results use the original dry-mass basis.


Do not subtract a blank twice or multiply its concentration by a dilution it never underwent. An uncertain or variable blank needs its own contribution to the uncertainty budget. “mg/L in digest” and “mg/kg dry material” are different results even when they refer to the same preparation.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Practical and transfer
Report both plant results, the full preparation calculation, QC interpretation and the role of the method blank. Explain why an elemental amount does not identify a molecular species. Identify missing recovery and uncertainty evidence before claiming a validated total-copper result.
A separate sample uses 0.2000 g dry material made to 25.00 mL. Its measured fivefold dilution gives 0.0800 mg/L Cu; the undiluted method-blank digest is 0.0100 mg/L. Calculate the blank-corrected dry-mass result.






Check the mass balance





The sample digest is \(0.0800\times5-0.0100=0.3900\) mg/L. It contains 0.009750 mg Cu, giving 48.75 mg/kg dry mass. The supplied A1 and A2 results are 160.36 and 300.42 mg/kg respectively, conditional on the stated recovery.

text:
Finish with the analytical argument
The final case provides new caffeine standards, sample responses, preparation records and an independent check. You will choose which results can be reported, identify the need for a new dilution or better separation, and write a reproducible conclusion. Keep the analytical question in view: caffeine mass concentration in each supplied beverage, not simply an area printed by software.



The chemical quantity and sample constraints determine which type of method can answer the question.


The case uses a supplied HPLC separation and UV response. The candidate peak has supporting standard-retention evidence and explicit separation decisions. The scenario assumes the accepted peaks represent caffeine. No instrument method is claimed to be validated for every beverage. The file dictionary records the assumptions behind the supplied flags and uncertainty inputs.

title: Choosing and defending a result
section: Decide on the method before fitting data
text:
Decide on the method before fitting data
An elemental method would destroy the molecular information needed to identify caffeine. A nonspecific single-wavelength absorbance of a complex drink could include several absorbing components. A suitable separation can make a detector response more selective. Method choice involves the required range, matrix, identity evidence, preparation recovery, uncertainty and available sample. The most sensitive instrument can still answer the wrong measurand.

title: Choosing and defending a result
section: Calibrate and check this independent dataset
text:
Calibrate and check this independent dataset

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
standards <- read_csv("data/course/case-standards.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fit <- lm(area ~ caffeine_mg_l, data = standards)
a <- unname(coef(fit)[1])
b <- unname(coef(fit)[2])
qc <- read_csv("data/course/case-qc.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(estimated_mg_l = (area - a) / b,
         recovery_percent = 100 * estimated_mg_l / reference_mg_l,
         pass = recovery_percent >= acceptance_low &
                  recovery_percent <= acceptance_high)
qc




The new case has its own calibration and range, separate from the earlier HPLC exercise.


The case line is area = 4 + 40 × concentration, valid over 0–30 mg/L under the supplied assumptions. The independent 15.00 mg/L check recovers about 100.67%, within the supplied 95–105% exercise window. These standards are deliberately idealised: their zero residual is not evidence of zero real measurement uncertainty. The case supplies separate standard uncertainties for final concentration estimates. Do not derive a perfect uncertainty from these rounded teaching points.

title: Choosing and defending a result
section: Make the decision before exporting a number
text:
Make the decision before exporting a number

samples <- read_csv("data/course/case-samples.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
results <- samples |>
  mutate(final_estimate_mg_l = (area - a) / b,
         in_range = final_estimate_mg_l >= 0 & final_estimate_mg_l <= 30,
         reportable = in_range & resolved & qc_pass & all(qc$pass),
         dilution_factor = final_ml / aliquot_ml,
         original_mg_l = if_else(reportable,
                                 final_estimate_mg_l * dilution_factor, NA_real_),
         u_original_mg_l = if_else(reportable,
           u_final_concentration_mg_l * dilution_factor, NA_real_),
         decision = case_when(!qc_pass | !all(qc$pass) ~ "withhold: QC",
                              !resolved ~ "withhold: coelution",
                              !in_range ~ "remeasure: outside range",
                              TRUE ~ "conditional result"))
results |> select(preparation_id, sample_id, original_mg_l, u_original_mg_l, decision)
write_csv(results, "output/final-case-results.csv", na = "NA")

C1 gives 15 mg/L in the final solution and 150 mg/L in drink A. C2 exceeds range and cannot establish drink B’s concentration. C3 is a new preparation of B using 2.00 mL made to 50.00 mL, rather than C2’s 5.00 mL. Its valid final estimate is 16 mg/L, yielding 400 mg/L original. C4 has an unresolved interfering peak and no reportable caffeine concentration despite passing range and QC.



Supported preparations have concentrations and scaled standard uncertainties; withheld ones do not appear as zero.


C1’s supplied final-concentration standard uncertainty is 0.15 mg/L and C3’s is 0.16 mg/L. Scaling by dilution gives 1.5 and 4.0 mg/L respectively. This is a limited budget, neglecting volumes, sampling and preparation recovery. The error bars are standard uncertainties, not 95% confidence intervals. Identify what would need to be established before claiming the full method’s uncertainty is fit for the intended decision.

title: Choosing and defending a result
section: Agreement is not the same as association
text:
Agreement is not the same as association
The comparison dataset measures six separate reference samples by HPLC and a nonspecific unseparated UV method. Both methods increase with reference concentration, but their differences tell different stories.

comparison <- read_csv("data/course/method-comparison.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(hplc_difference = hplc_mg_l - reference_mg_l,
         uv_difference = nonspecific_uv_mg_l - reference_mg_l)
ggplot(comparison, aes(reference_mg_l, uv_difference)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Reference result (mg/L)", y = "Unseparated UV minus reference (mg/L)") +
  theme_minimal()




The nonspecific method’s positive discrepancy grows with concentration, whereas the HPLC discrepancy is much smaller.


A high correlation would not establish interchangeability or acceptable bias. The pattern may motivate matrix/selectivity investigations; the plot alone does not prove the chemical cause. Reference uncertainty, sample scope and the required performance must be considered before accepting a method comparison.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
Where mass spectrometry adds evidence



An ion source creates ions; a mass analyser separates or filters m/z; a detector records abundance.


A mass spectrometer measures ions by mass-to-charge, not neutral molecular mass directly. In positive electrospray a singly protonated caffeine ion can occur near \(m/z\) 195, whereas neutral caffeine has nominal mass 194. Multiple charges, adducts and fragments change the interpretation. Chromatography-MS combines a retention dimension with ion information, but an ion signal still needs a suitable calibration for quantification. Waters guide to ionisation and mass-to-charge



An illustrative ion spectrum is a teaching pattern, not an authentic library match for caffeine.


Do not identify a molecule from a single nominal mass or from this deliberately illustrative spectrum. Authentic reference spectra, exact-mass or fragmentation evidence where appropriate, blanks and suitable standards can strengthen an identity claim. More instrument detail is optional here: the core task is to understand which evidence addresses identity and which addresses amount.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
Your final report
Use the supplied course-report.Rmd template at the project root. Include the measurand and sample scope; preparation factors; calibration direction and range; QC results; a table of supported results and explicit withheld reasons; standard uncertainty with its omissions; and a conclusion explaining the next action for each unresolved sample. Explain what evidence supports caffeine identity.
Render after restarting R. Ask a peer to render from the original data in a new folder. A reader should be able to follow a reported number back to the signal, preparation record and chemical assumption. Do not replace the chemical interpretation with a pasted R summary.
For a new accepted sample with area 804 and a 4.00 mL aliquot made to 40.00 mL, calculate original concentration. Then explain what changes if its integration window contains an unresolved second absorbing compound.






Check your result and next action





Final concentration is \((804-4)/40=20\) mg/L and the factor is 10, giving 200 mg/L original, conditional on the stated method and accepted evidence. With an unresolved contributing compound, that area no longer supports the same caffeine estimate. Improve separation or obtain justified additional selective evidence before reporting it.

title: GC and HPLC
section: Choose how the analyte can enter and move
text:
Choose how the analyte can enter and move
Gas chromatography carries a vapour in a gas; liquid chromatography carries solute in a liquid. Both use differential interaction with a stationary phase, then detect the arriving components. Method choice must account for sample introduction, stability, selectivity, matrix and detection, not just whether a column is available.



Carrier gas moves a vaporised sample through an oven-controlled GC column to a detector.


Conventional GC suits analytes that can enter the gas phase and tolerate the relevant introduction and separation conditions. Headspace can introduce volatile components above a complex sample; the entire matrix need not be volatile. Temperature programming changes retention over a run. Stationary phase chemistry also matters: boiling point alone does not define retention. Agilent introduction to headspace sampling



HPLC pumps a controlled liquid mobile phase through an injected sample and packed column.


HPLC can accommodate many analytes unsuited to ordinary GC, provided they are soluble and stable under the chosen conditions. In reversed-phase HPLC a relatively nonpolar stationary phase interacts with solutes in a more polar mobile phase. Increasing organic modifier often reduces retention of suitably retained compounds, but ionisation, solvent choice and analyte chemistry affect the actual behaviour.

title: GC and HPLC
section: A program belongs to a complete method
text:
A program belongs to a complete method
An isocratic LC run keeps mobile-phase composition fixed. A gradient changes composition during the run. The supplied illustrative program begins at 10% organic, rises to 70%, holds, then returns to 10% and re-equilibrates before the next injection. It is not a validated caffeine method or a pump setup instruction.



The illustrative gradient includes a return to initial conditions and time for re-equilibration.


Flow, column, temperature, injection solvent and detector settings also belong to the method. Changing them can alter retention or response. A retention-time comparison made under a different method is not a controlled identification comparison.
A flame-ionisation detector measures an ion-current response useful for many organic compounds in GC. A UV detector measures absorbance for compounds that absorb at the chosen wavelength. MS records ions separated by mass-to-charge. These responses differ in selectivity and response factors. A chromatographic area is not a universal count of molecules.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Calibrate integrated caffeine peak area
The simulated HPLC standards have known caffeine concentration in the final solution. Peak areas are supplied from integration, not calculated by counting CSV rows. Assume adequate separation, an appropriate baseline, and a linear response over 0–40 mg/L for this example.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
standards <- read_csv("data/course/hplc-standards.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fit_external <- lm(caffeine_area ~ caffeine_mg_l, data = standards)
coef(fit_external)




External calibration relates integrated caffeine area to final-solution concentration.


The fitted relationship is area = 3 + 50 × concentration. Area depends on the introduced analyte amount and detector response. If an injection introduces less of the same solution, an external-area calibration can give a different estimated concentration even though the vial concentration did not change.

title: GC and HPLC
section: Use an internal standard for a specific shared effect
text:
Use an internal standard for a specific shared effect
An internal standard is a distinguishable compound added in known amount. In this exercise every final standard and sample has 10 mg/L internal standard. Assume resolved peaks and sufficiently similar responses to a shared injection variation. Calibrate the analyte/internal-standard area ratio against analyte concentration under that fixed internal-standard concentration.



The standard and analyte share selected measurement steps; the calibrated ratio can cancel common variation.



standards <- standards |>
  mutate(area_ratio = caffeine_area / internal_standard_area)
fit_ratio <- lm(area_ratio ~ caffeine_mg_l, data = standards)
injections <- read_csv("data/course/hplc-injections.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(area_ratio = caffeine_area / internal_standard_area,
         final_external_mg_l = (caffeine_area - coef(fit_external)[1]) /
                                 coef(fit_external)[2],
         final_ratio_mg_l = (area_ratio - coef(fit_ratio)[1]) /
                              coef(fit_ratio)[2])
injections |> select(injection_id, preparation_id, final_external_mg_l,
                      final_ratio_mg_l)




Area-ratio calibration requires matched internal-standard concentration and a retained intercept.


I1 and I2 are repeated injections of D1. External-area estimates are 15.00 and 12.00 mg/L. Area-ratio estimates are 15.000 and 15.015 mg/L: a shared injection effect has mostly cancelled. The small difference remains because the simulated signals include a response offset. This is useful compensation, not exact invariance under every error.



Two injections of the same preparation agree much better after the matched ratio correction.


An internal standard cannot repair analyte extraction loss that occurred before it was added. It also cannot resolve overlapping peaks or cancel an effect that changes analyte and standard differently. If its concentration differs between standards and samples, this simple ratio-versus-concentration calibration needs a different concentration-ratio model. Manufacturer discussion of calibration approaches

title: GC and HPLC
section: Guard results with separation, QC and range evidence
text:
Guard results with separation, QC and range evidence

results <- injections |>
  mutate(in_range = final_ratio_mg_l >= 0 & final_ratio_mg_l <= 40,
         reportable = resolved & qc_pass & in_range,
         original_mg_l = if_else(reportable,
                                 final_ratio_mg_l * dilution_factor, NA_real_))
results |> select(injection_id, preparation_id, original_mg_l, reportable)
write_csv(results, "output/hplc-results.csv", na = "NA")

The accepted D1 preparation gives about 150 mg/L in the supplied drink after its tenfold dilution. I3’s candidate caffeine peak is not resolved; I4 belongs to a failed QC condition. Both have withheld concentration results despite algebraically calculable ratios. The supplied flags represent decisions from the exercise’s separation and QC evidence; in real work they must come from records, not convenient booleans assigned after seeing an answer.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Practical and transfer
Compare GC and HPLC for a volatile solvent mixture and an aqueous mixture of nonvolatile, heat-sensitive compounds. Explain how matrix and detector choice could change your answer. Report external and internal-standard estimates for D1, while distinguishing a repeated injection from a new preparation.
For transfer, a new accepted injection has caffeine area 903, internal-standard area 600, internal-standard concentration 10 mg/L and dilution factor 5. Use the fitted ratio model to estimate the original concentration. Would you use that answer if its caffeine peak overlapped a matrix peak?






Numerical and decision checks





The ratio is 1.505 and the fitted ratio relation is \(R=0.006+0.100c\). Final caffeine is 14.99 mg/L, giving 74.95 mg/L original. An unresolved contributing matrix peak invalidates that simple analyte-area interpretation; the ratio is not a cure for coelution.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
section: A voltage depends on the complete cell
text:
A voltage depends on the complete cell
A potentiometric measurement compares an indicator electrode with a reference electrode using a high-input-impedance meter. The useful analytical response is a potential difference at negligible net measurement current. A combined pH electrode packages both functions together; it does not eliminate the reference. You will fit a log-concentration calibration, invert it, and use an independent check to detect a later drift.



An indicator and reference electrode contact the sample and connect to a high-impedance meter.


The indicator membrane responds preferentially to a chemical species. The reference provides a comparatively stable potential and contacts the sample through a junction. Membrane state, junction conditions, temperature and interfering ions can affect the measured voltage. A number in mV is not a concentration until a suitable relation and calibration are established.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
section: Activity explains why matching conditions matters
text:
Activity explains why matching conditions matters
For an ideal ion-selective response,
\[E=K+\frac{2.303RT}{zF}\log_{10}a_i\]
Here \(z\) is the signed ion charge and \(a_i\) is dimensionless activity, related to concentration by \(a_i=\gamma_i c_i/c^\circ\). At 25 °C the ideal magnitude for a monovalent ion is about 59.16 mV per decade. With this potential convention an anion such as fluoride has a negative slope. Instrument polarity and cell conventions should always be stated rather than guessed from a sign. HORIBA electrode principle



Activity depends on concentration and its activity coefficient; matched conditions support calibration transfer.


A concentration calibration assumes the activity relationship is sufficiently consistent between standards and samples. An ionic-strength adjustment can help under a specified procedure; it does not make every interference disappear. Do not equate free-ion response with total element concentration when complexes, precipitation or different species are present.
For hydrogen ion, pH is \(-\log_{10}a_{H^+}\). A one-unit increase means a tenfold activity decrease. Calibrate a pH system with appropriate buffers at the measurement temperature, and check performance across the required range.



An ideal pH response is linear in pH, which is already a logarithmic activity quantity.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
section: Fit the fluoride data in logarithmic coordinates
text:
Fit the fluoride data in logarithmic coordinates
These standards have supplied fluoride concentrations in mol/L under matched ionic-strength conditions at 25 °C. Their response is linear over the stated \(10^{-5}\)–\(10^{-3}\) mol/L range. That is a scenario assumption, not a universal range for every fluoride electrode.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
standards <- read_csv("data/course/electrode-standards.csv",
                      show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(log_c = log10(fluoride_mol_l))
fit <- lm(potential_mv ~ log_c, data = standards)
a <- unname(coef(fit)[1])
b <- unname(coef(fit)[2])
coef(fit)
ggplot(standards, aes(log_c, potential_mv)) +
  geom_point() + geom_abline(intercept = a, slope = b) +
  labs(x = "log10[c / (1 mol/L)]", y = "Potential (mV)") +
  theme_minimal()




The fitted fluoride response has slope about −59.10 mV per concentration decade.


log10() takes a logarithm, not a new unit conversion. Numerically we use the value of concentration expressed in mol/L relative to 1 mol/L. If you change the concentration unit without changing the calibration intercept, the inverse estimate will be wrong. Zero and negative concentrations have no finite logarithm; they cannot be used as ordinary log-calibration points.



The same standards do not form a straight line on an untransformed concentration axis.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Undo the logarithm after inversion
The fitted model is \(E=a+b\log_{10}[c/(1\,\mathrm{mol/L})]\). First calculate \((E-a)/b\), then raise 10 to that power. For a 121.2 mV measurement in the accepted early block, the estimate is about \(2.00\times10^{-4}\) mol/L.

unknown_mv <- 121.2
unknown_mol_l <- 10^((unknown_mv - a) / b)
in_range <- unknown_mol_l >= min(standards$fluoride_mol_l) &
            unknown_mol_l <= max(standards$fluoride_mol_l)
c(unknown_mol_l = unknown_mol_l, in_range = in_range)

A tenfold change is about 59 mV here; a twofold change is about 17.8 mV. Voltage uncertainty maps multiplicatively to concentration. Symmetric voltage limits generally become asymmetric concentration limits after exponentiation. Do not attach a voltage SD directly to a concentration result.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
A late check detects drift
The check material is \(1.00\times10^{-4}\) mol/L. A supplied exercise rule accepts an absolute potential error no greater than 2.0 mV. This is a check rule for the example, not a universal electrode specification.

checks <- read_csv("data/course/electrode-checks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(expected_mv = a + b * log10(check_fluoride_mol_l),
         error_mv = potential_mv - expected_mv,
         check_pass = abs(error_mv) <= allowed_abs_error_mv)
checks
write_csv(checks, "output/electrode-checks.csv")




The early check differs by about 0.12 mV; the later check differs by about 6.02 mV and fails.


Do not report the late sample from the earlier calibration after this failure. Investigate electrode conditioning, reference/junction effects, temperature and sample/standard conditions as appropriate; establish satisfactory calibration and checks, then remeasure. A changed voltage alone does not identify which cause occurred.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Place other electrochemical methods
Potentiometry reads potential with negligible measurement current. Amperometry reads current under specified potential conditions. Voltammetry records current while varying potential, and coulometry measures charge. Their signals therefore require different models. In coulometry the ideal amount relationship \(n=Q/(zF)\) also requires the intended reaction to account for the charge. A current reading is not a pH measurement with a different unit.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Practical and transfer
Save the calibration coefficients, early concentration and check table. Explain the activity/concentration assumption, slope sign, inverse calculation and reason for withholding the later result. Compare the same calibration on linear and logarithmic concentration axes.
For transfer, decrease the accepted sample voltage by 17.8 mV using the fitted line. Predict the concentration factor before calculating it. Is a result for free fluoride necessarily total fluorine in a complex sample?






Check the result





The factor is \(10^{-17.8/(-59.10)}\approx2.001\), so the estimate is about \(4.00\times10^{-4}\) mol/L. A free-ion-responsive procedure does not establish total fluorine across all chemical forms.

title: Sampling and preparation
section: Does the aliquot represent the material?
text:
Does the aliquot represent the material?
A precise instrument only measures what reaches it. If you take all your material from the top of a heterogeneous container, repeating the measurement will not discover what is at the bottom. This unit follows the sample from the sampling target through preparation to a reported mass fraction. You will use R to preserve preparation identities and reverse each dilution and extraction step.



The top, middle and bottom have different concentrations in a deliberately heterogeneous material.


The supplied strata have equal masses. Their mean concentrations are 8, 14 and 25 mg Fe/kg, giving an equal-mass overall mean of 15.67 mg/kg. Sampling only the top would give about 8 mg/kg even if every measurement were extremely precise. If the stratum masses differed, the simple average would be wrong: use the known mass fractions. If those fractions are unknown, more arithmetic cannot supply them.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
grabs <- read_csv("data/course/sampling.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
strata <- grabs |>
  group_by(position) |>
  summarise(mean_mg_kg = mean(iron_mg_kg), .groups = "drop")
strata
equal_mass_mean <- mean(strata$mean_mg_kg)
equal_mass_mean




Within-stratum repeatability is much smaller than the difference between positions.


A composite can combine increments in specified proportions to estimate a bulk quantity. It also hides the original spatial variation: one composite is not several independent samples. Decide whether the question concerns a bulk mean, variation among locations, or a maximum before combining material. Sampling contributes to uncertainty when the result refers beyond the material actually measured. Eurachem sampling guidance

title: Sampling and preparation
section: Preserve the quantity you intend to measure
text:
Preserve the quantity you intend to measure
During storage, oxidation, precipitation, adsorption and biological processes can alter composition. A preservation treatment must fit the intended measurand. Acidifying an elemental-analysis sample can help retain material in solution, but it does not preserve every original chemical species. Record collection, container, treatment and elapsed time with the sample ID.



Chemical reactions, surfaces and biological processes can change a stored sample.


Filtration, extraction and digestion do different things. Filtration separates material by a stated operation. Extraction transfers accessible analyte to another phase. Digestion breaks down material for an elemental measurement, and can destroy molecular information. None guarantees complete recovery just because the resulting solution is clear.

title: Sampling and preparation
text:
Back-calculate an extraction
The supplied caffeine exercise starts with a weighed dry teaching material. Assume no analyte loss in transfer and that the reported final concentration is valid for the prepared solution. We call the result extracted caffeine: complete recovery of native caffeine has not been independently established.



A weighed sample gives an extract, then a diluted aliquot for measurement.


For T1a, 0.5000 g material gives 25.00 mL extract; 2.00 mL of that extract is made to 10.00 mL. The final concentration is 1.92 mg/L. Work backwards:
\[c_{extract}=c_{final}\frac{V_{final}}{V_{aliquot}},\qquad
m_{extracted}=c_{extract}V_{extract},\qquad
w_{extracted}=\frac{m_{extracted}}{m_{sample}}\]
The extract is 9.60 mg/L, containing 0.240 mg caffeine. Dividing by 0.5000 g gives 0.480 mg/g. The extract volume must be in litres when multiplying mg/L.

prep <- read_csv("data/course/extractions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(prep$preparation_id),
          all(prep$mass_g > 0), all(prep$aliquot_ml > 0))
results <- prep |>
  mutate(extract_mg_l = final_caffeine_mg_l * final_ml / aliquot_ml,
         extracted_mg = extract_mg_l * extract_ml / 1000,
         caffeine_mg_g = extracted_mg / mass_g)
results
write_csv(results, "output/extracted-caffeine.csv")




Independent preparations give extracted caffeine per gram, rather than concentration in the measured flask.


T1a and T1b are independent preparations from the same supplied material T1. T2a comes from another supplied material. Do not describe three preparations as three independently obtained materials. Keep sample ID, preparation ID and reading ID separate so later joins preserve the correct mass and volumes.

title: Sampling and preparation
text:
Why can several extractions help?
For two immiscible phases at an ideal equilibrium, let \(D=c_{extracting}/c_{aqueous}\). The fraction left in an aqueous volume \(V_a\) after extraction with volume \(V_o\) is \(V_a/(V_a+D V_o)\). This follows by writing the total analyte amount as \(c_aV_a+(D c_a)V_o\).



The distribution ratio describes concentrations, while recovery also depends on phase volumes.


For \(D=9\), 20 mL aqueous phase and 10 mL extracting phase, recovery is 81.8%. Two successive 5 mL extractions leave the fraction \([20/(20+9\times5)]^2\), giving 90.5% total recovery with the same total solvent volume. These ideal calculations assume equilibrium, constant phase volumes, no reaction, and complete separation between extractions. Real emulsions, incomplete equilibration, ionisation and bound analyte can change recovery.

one_recovery <- 1 - 20 / (20 + 9 * 10)
two_recovery <- 1 - (20 / (20 + 9 * 5))^2
100 * c(one = one_recovery, two = two_recovery)




Two smaller ideal extractions recover more than one extraction with the same total solvent.

title: Sampling and preparation
text:
Practical and transfer
Report the three extracted-caffeine results, the complete volume chain, and which assumptions prevent you from claiming total native caffeine. Add a sampling diagram for a heterogeneous material and explain whether your target is a bulk mean or spatial variation.
For a new preparation, 0.4000 g material is extracted to 40.00 mL. A 1.00 mL aliquot made to 10.00 mL gives 1.50 mg/L. Calculate extracted caffeine in mg/g. Then explain whether a successful spike after extraction proves complete extraction of native analyte.






Check your result and interpretation





The new extract contains 15.0 mg/L × 0.04000 L = 0.600 mg, or 1.50 mg/g. A spike added after extraction does not pass through the extraction step and cannot establish its recovery. The supplied results are 0.480, 0.490 and 0.750 mg/g. These are extracted amounts under the given preparation.



Before moving on, explain why top-only sampling can be biased despite a tiny SD, why the same total solvent can give different recovery, and why a retained raw preparation table is part of the analytical evidence.

title: Equilibrium and titration
section: Use a reaction to count analyte
text:
Use a reaction to count analyte
In a titration, a standardised reagent reacts with a known sample portion. Its concentration and delivered volume establish the amount consumed. The chemical reaction converts that amount to analyte amount. A signal change identifies an endpoint intended to estimate the stoichiometric equivalence point. The two are related but not identical by definition.
You will calculate a strong-acid concentration, inspect pH curves, and report an EDTA hardness result with its stated equivalent basis.



A burette delivers a measured volume of standardised titrant to a known sample aliquot.


Read the initial and final burette positions. Delivered volume is their difference, not the final reading alone. Remove any justified method-blank consumption on the same volume basis. Titrant concentration must be established: we supply a standardised value rather than assuming a nominal bottle label is exact. Meniscus reading, transfer, standardisation and endpoint detection all contribute uncertainty.

title: Equilibrium and titration
section: Strong acid and base give a simple amount balance
text:
Strong acid and base give a simple amount balance
For \(\mathrm{H^++OH^-\rightarrow H_2O}\), the equivalence condition is \(n_{acid}=n_{base}\). With an acid aliquot \(V_a\) and standardised base concentration \(c_b\), \(c_a=c_bV_{eq}/V_a\) for this 1:1 reaction.
The example uses 25.00 mL acid and 0.1000 mol/L base. A supplied endpoint estimate of 25.00 mL gives 0.1000 mol/L acid. Volumes can be in the same unit in their ratio; converting to amounts in mol requires litres.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
curve <- read_csv("data/course/acid-titration.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ggplot(curve, aes(volume_ml, ph)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "0.1000 mol/L base added (mL)", y = "pH") +
  theme_minimal()
c_acid <- 0.1000 * 25.00 / 25.00
c_acid




The ideal strong-acid curve changes rapidly near the equivalence volume.


Before equivalence, excess acid controls pH; after it, excess base does. Near neutrality the water equilibrium matters, so a naive subtraction followed by -log10(0) fails. The generator includes water autoionisation and charge balance at 25 °C. At equivalence this ideal strong-acid/strong-base system has pH 7; that is not a universal titration rule.

title: Equilibrium and titration
section: An endpoint is an estimate with a procedure
text:
An endpoint is an estimate with a procedure
The steep part makes a small volume change observable. An indicator changes colour over a pH interval; choose one whose transition is appropriate to the curve and desired endpoint accuracy. An electrode gives a series from which an endpoint algorithm can be defined. A slope maximum is a useful exploratory check, not a proof of a chemically correct endpoint.

slopes <- data.frame(
  midpoint_ml = (head(curve$volume_ml, -1) + tail(curve$volume_ml, -1)) / 2,
  ph_per_ml = diff(curve$ph) / diff(curve$volume_ml))
ggplot(slopes, aes(midpoint_ml, ph_per_ml)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Midpoint of addition interval (mL)", y = "Change in pH per mL") +
  theme_minimal()

diff() subtracts consecutive values. Divide by the actual volume difference: our additions are more closely spaced near equivalence. Treating every row as one millilitre would give a distorted derivative. Differencing also amplifies measurement noise, so a real procedure needs a specified endpoint method.



Finite differences identify a steep region, with the volume spacing included explicitly.


For a weak acid, its conjugate base affects pH at equivalence. Before equivalence a buffer region can appear. The comparison below uses the same initial amount and base, with supplied pKa 4.76 for the weak acid.



Strong and weak acids share the same equivalence volume here but not the same pH curve.


The equivalent amount follows stoichiometry; pH follows the equilibrium composition. A weaker acid does not automatically require less base if its initial amount is the same. Use the curve to reason about indicator choice, not to redefine the reaction stoichiometry.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
EDTA counts metal equivalents
EDTA forms a 1:1 complex with each accessible metal ion in this simplified hardness exercise. Its protonation and the metal’s competing reactions affect the effective binding under the chosen conditions. A pH buffer supports a large enough conditional formation constant and an appropriate indicator response. Merely writing the overall formation constant is not enough to establish performance at every pH.



One EDTA molecule binds one metal ion; hardness is then expressed on an equivalent CaCO₃ mass basis.


Assume the supplied titration selectively counts Ca and Mg under its specified buffer/indicator conditions. The combined amount is reported as CaCO₃, using 100.09 g/mol. This does not identify Ca and Mg individually or establish that carbonate is present. Other accessible metals or masked species can change which quantity the procedure measures.

hardness <- read_csv("data/course/edta.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(delivered_ml = final_burette_ml - initial_burette_ml,
         corrected_ml = delivered_ml - blank_ml,
         moles_metal = edta_mol_l * corrected_ml / 1000,
         hardness_mg_l_CaCO3 = moles_metal * 100.09 * 1000 /
                                (sample_ml / 1000))
hardness
write_csv(hardness, "output/hardness.csv")

H1a delivers 6.20 mL; subtracting the 0.05 mL blank leaves 6.15 mL. At 0.01000 mol/L this is \(6.15\times10^{-5}\) mol in 50.00 mL sample, or 123.11 mg/L as CaCO₃. H1b is another preparation of H1, not another independently obtained water.



Hardness results preserve preparation identity and the explicit CaCO₃ reporting basis.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Practical and transfer
Report the acid concentration, pH curve, finite-difference interpretation and three hardness results. Explain which volume is an endpoint estimate and why “pH 7” is not a general endpoint rule. List the assumptions connecting EDTA consumption to Ca/Mg hardness and one relevant source of uncertainty beyond repeatability.
A new 25.00 mL water sample consumes 4.10 mL EDTA after the initial/final burette subtraction. A matched blank consumes 0.10 mL; EDTA is 0.01000 mol/L. Calculate hardness, then predict the direction of error from forgetting the blank.






Numerical and chemical checks





Corrected volume is 4.00 mL, giving 160.14 mg/L as CaCO₃. Omitting the blank biases the result high in this consumption model. Supplied results: H1a 123.11, H1b 124.11 and H2a 191.17 mg/L as CaCO₃. A weak-acid equivalence point can have pH above 7 despite 1:1 neutralisation.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Which information survives atomisation?

Absorption moves an atom from lower to higher energy, while emission releases a photon during a transition from higher to lower energy.An element amount can survive; original molecular identity generally does not.

A plant copper result is not evidence of the original copper-binding molecule or oxidation state.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Absorption supplies the photon

Absorption moves an atom from lower to higher energy, while emission releases a photon during a transition from higher to lower energy.A source photon promotes a suitable free atom to a higher state.

Energy must match an allowed transition. The relevant population depends on atomisation conditions.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Emission releases the photon

Absorption moves an atom from lower to higher energy, while emission releases a photon during a transition from higher to lower energy.An excited population emits characteristic light during transitions.

Excitation is supplied by the atomisation/excitation environment. Not every introduced atom contributes the same response regardless of matrix.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Follow the AAS path

The sample must be converted into an appropriate free-atom population; flame and graphite furnace differ in how this is achieved.Element source → atomiser → selected wavelength → detector.

The detector compares transmitted source light. Do not describe flame emission alone as the AAS measured signal.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
The flame introduces material continuously

Flame AAS, graphite furnace AAS and ICP optical emission differ in introduction, atomisation and detection conditions.Transport and atomisation affect sensitivity.

The selected source/wavelength, sample introduction and matrix compatibility belong to the measurement method.

title: Atomic measurements
section: The graphite furnace treats a small aliquot
text:
The graphite furnace treats a small aliquot

Flame AAS, graphite furnace AAS and ICP optical emission differ in introduction, atomisation and detection conditions.A heating program separates drying, matrix removal and atomisation.

Small volume and high sensitivity are not guarantees against matrix effects. Discuss the different introduction strategy without an exhaustive furnace-design survey.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Follow the ICP optical-emission path

Elemental emission does not preserve the original molecular identity or oxidation-state distribution of the sample.Aerosol → plasma excitation → wavelength separation → detector.

This measures emitted light. It is not ICP-MS, which detects ions by mass-to-charge.

title: Atomic measurements
section: Many elements means many possible lines
text:
Many elements means many possible lines

Elemental emission does not preserve the original molecular identity or oxidation-state distribution of the sample.Line choice and background still matter.

Multielement capability does not imply zero spectral overlap or zero matrix effects.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Look around the target line

An illustrative neighbouring emission feature changes the spectrum around a target line; profiles are not identification references.Which signal would a broad integration window include?

The illustrative neighbouring feature can bias the selected line measurement. These are simulated profiles, not reference identification spectra.

title: Atomic measurements
section: An interference need not look like a separate peak
text:
An interference need not look like a separate peak

An illustrative neighbouring emission feature changes the spectrum around a target line; profiles are not identification references.Transport and chemical effects can change the target population.

A stable reading does not prove correct recovery. Alternative lines, matrix-matched checks and suitable validation can address different issues.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Calibrate the introduced solution

Copper emission counts increase approximately linearly over zero to two mg/L in introduced solution.Concentration axis: mg copper/L measured solution.

The solution is not yet on a dry-material basis. Fit counts as response and retain the intercept.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Check with independent material

Two independent dissolved copper checks recover about 100.4 and 100.8 percent, within the exercise window.Both supplied checks meet the exercise 95–105% rule.

Recoveries are about 100.37 and 100.77 percent. They test the check solution conditions, not plant digestion completeness.

title: Atomic measurements
section: Trace the sample mass and volumes
text:
Trace the sample mass and volumes

A1: (0.40189 × 2 − 0.001992) mg/L × 0.05000 L / 0.0002500 kg = 160.36 mg/kg dry mass.A1: 0.2500 g dry material → 50.00 mL digest → twofold dilution.

No full recovery validation is supplied. Result is conditional on quantitative transfer and digestion under the scenario.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Convert the sample signal

Copper emission counts increase approximately linearly over zero to two mg/L in introduced solution.A1 measured solution ≈ 0.40189 mg/L copper.

The calibration response range is zero to two mg/L. Check introduced solution concentration before back-calculating.

title: Atomic measurements
section: The method blank has a different dilution history
text:
The method blank has a different dilution history

A blank, independent reference check and a sample spike examine different parts of the measurement.Blank digest is measured undiluted.

Its measured concentration is about 0.0019922 mg/L. The sample has a further factor of two, but the blank does not.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Subtract on a common basis

A1: (0.40189 × 2 − 0.001992) mg/L × 0.05000 L / 0.0002500 kg = 160.36 mg/kg dry mass.A1 digest: 0.40189 × 2 − 0.001992 = 0.80179 mg/L.

First undo sample dilution, then subtract blank digest concentration. Multiplying a blank by a dilution it never underwent would be wrong.

title: Atomic measurements
section: Recover amount, then divide by original mass
text:
Recover amount, then divide by original mass

Conditional copper dry-mass results are about 160 and 300 mg/kg in two supplied plant samples.0.80179 mg/L × 0.05000 L / 0.0002500 kg = 160.36 mg/kg dry.

Ask students to cancel units. A concentration in digest and a mass fraction in original material are different quantities.

title: Atomic measurements
section: A blank has no sample mass denominator
text:
A blank has no sample mass denominator

Conditional copper dry-mass results are about 160 and 300 mg/kg in two supplied plant samples.No mg/kg plant result is assigned to the method blank.

Preserve its preparation role and report blank evidence without pretending it is a zero-mass sample concentration.

title: Atomic measurements
section: Passing a dissolved check cannot prove digestion recovery
text:
Passing a dissolved check cannot prove digestion recovery

Two independent dissolved copper checks recover about 100.4 and 100.8 percent, within the exercise window.What material would better challenge the whole preparation?

A suitable reference material and/or appropriate recovery study, with evidence that the measurand and matrix are relevant.

title: Atomic measurements
section: Uncertainty needs more than counting noise
text:
Uncertainty needs more than counting noise

Averaging repeated readings reduces independent reading noise; it does not remove a common stock or preparation effect.Mass, volume, calibration, blank variation and recovery can all contribute.

The worked elemental result is a conditional point estimate. Do not invent a complete uncertainty from the few numbers given.

title: Atomic measurements
section: Choose among instruments for the question
text:
Choose among instruments for the question

Flame AAS, graphite furnace AAS and ICP optical emission differ in introduction, atomisation and detection conditions.Range, matrix, elements, sample volume, throughput and required uncertainty.

Avoid a universal ranking that declares one instrument best. Revisit flame, furnace and plasma differences.

title: Atomic measurements
section: Transfer the blank and dry-mass basis
text:
Transfer the blank and dry-mass basis

A1: (0.40189 × 2 − 0.001992) mg/L × 0.05000 L / 0.0002500 kg = 160.36 mg/kg dry mass.0.2000 g to 25.00 mL; fivefold dilution reads 0.0800 mg/L; blank digest 0.0100 mg/L.

Corrected digest is 0.3900 mg/L. Result is 48.75 mg/kg dry mass. Require the blank and dilution order.
