title: Choosing and defending a result
section: Start with the claim you need to defend
text:
Start with the claim you need to defend

Different analytical questions call for elemental detection, molecular separation, titration or ion-activity measurement.Caffeine concentration in supplied drinks, with explicit limitations.

This case uses an independent calibration and new preparation records. Do not reuse old coefficients simply because the analyte has the same name.

title: Choosing and defending a result
section: Choose a method for the chemical quantity
text:
Choose a method for the chemical quantity

Different analytical questions call for elemental detection, molecular separation, titration or ion-activity measurement.Elemental copper and molecular caffeine require different evidence.

An atomising elemental technique cannot preserve the molecular identity needed to establish caffeine.

title: Choosing and defending a result
section: A selective enough signal still needs calibration
text:
A selective enough signal still needs calibration

In reversed-phase HPLC, changing organic modifier often changes retention. Re-equilibrate before the next injection.Separation, identity evidence and response calibration work together.

The case supplies retention evidence and separation flags. They support a conditional caffeine interpretation under the stated scenario.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
Read this calibration and range

The independent final-case line is area equals four plus forty times caffeine concentration, over zero to thirty mg/L.Area = 4 + 40 × concentration; 0–30 mg/L final.

These are idealised teaching standards. Their zero residual does not imply zero real uncertainty; separate uncertainty inputs are supplied.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
Check independently before using it

A blank, independent reference check and a sample spike examine different parts of the measurement.The 15.00 mg/L check recovers 100.67%.

The supplied acceptance window is ninety-five to one hundred five percent. Passing this check does not validate every matrix or recovery step.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
Inspect preparation history

C3 supports 400 mg caffeine/L original under the stated conditions. The old out-of-range C2 reading remains unsupported.Which factor applies to each sample?

C1 and C2 use five millilitres to fifty; C3 uses a new two millilitre aliquot to fifty. C3 is new evidence, not an edited factor on C2.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
C1 supports a conditional result

The independent final-case line is area equals four plus forty times caffeine concentration, over zero to thirty mg/L.Area 604 → 15 mg/L final → 150 mg/L drink A.

The ratio of final to aliquot volume is ten. Check range, separation and QC in addition to the arithmetic.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
C2 needs a new measurement

The independent final-case line is area equals four plus forty times caffeine concentration, over zero to thirty mg/L.Area 1604 gives a candidate 40 mg/L final, outside range.

The code may calculate a candidate for diagnostic purposes, but the exported reportable concentration must be withheld.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
C3 supplies that new preparation

C3 supports 400 mg caffeine/L original under the stated conditions. The old out-of-range C2 reading remains unsupported.Area 644 → 16 mg/L final; factor 25 → 400 mg/L drink B.

C3 is within range and adequately separated under the scenario. Do not retroactively accept C2 as valid extrapolation.

title: Choosing and defending a result
section: C4 fails selectivity despite passing range
text:
C4 fails selectivity despite passing range

The same component areas appear resolved or overlapping when their retention-time spacing changes.An unresolved component contributes to the integrated peak.

Withhold the caffeine amount. Better separation or justified selective evidence is needed; a larger number of decimal places adds no information.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
Export decisions with the values

The result applies to a defined material under a defined procedure; the signal alone does not define the measurand.Withheld results are missing estimates with reasons, not zero concentrations.

The output CSV should retain preparation ID, original sample ID, factor and decision. A later reader should be able to audit the result.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
Read the uncertainty bars correctly

Accepted preparations give 150 and 400 mg/L original caffeine; bars show limited scaled standard uncertainties.C1: standard uncertainty 1.5 mg/L. C3: 4.0 mg/L.

These scale supplied final-concentration standard uncertainties by dilution. They are not ninety-five percent limits and omit volumes and preparation recovery.

title: Choosing and defending a result
section: Do not infer perfect uncertainty from rounded ideal data
text:
Do not infer perfect uncertainty from rounded ideal data

The independent final-case line is area equals four plus forty times caffeine concentration, over zero to thirty mg/L.A zero calibration residual does not prove a perfect method.

The case deliberately supplies standard uncertainties independently. Require an account of missing sources before a fit-for-purpose claim.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
Compare methods through discrepancies

Nonspecific UV positive discrepancies grow with reference concentration; HPLC discrepancies remain much smaller.Does a strong association establish agreement?

No. A biased method can track concentration closely. Examine differences and performance requirements.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
A concentration-dependent difference needs investigation

Nonspecific UV positive discrepancies grow with reference concentration; HPLC discrepancies remain much smaller.The nonspecific UV discrepancy grows across reference samples.

It may motivate selectivity and matrix investigations. The graph alone does not prove the underlying chemical cause. Reference uncertainty matters.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
What does MS contribute?

For a singly protonated molecule, [M+H]⁺ is about one mass unit above neutral M. Fragments and multiple charges require interpretation.Ions carry information about mass-to-charge and fragmentation.

The optional overview clarifies identity evidence and coupled detectors. It is not a new quantitative workflow or an exhaustive analyser survey.

title: Choosing and defending a result
section: The source determines which ions can appear
text:
The source determines which ions can appear

For a singly protonated molecule, [M+H]⁺ is about one mass unit above neutral M. Fragments and multiple charges require interpretation.Neutral molecular mass is not automatically the observed m/z.

Electrospray can produce protonated molecules and other ions; multiple charge states, adducts and fragments need interpretation.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
Interpret one plausible caffeine ion

Illustrative ion sticks include m/z 195; the pattern is not an authentic caffeine library spectrum.Nominal neutral mass 194; singly protonated [M+H]⁺ near m/z 195.

Do not call m/z 195 universal proof of caffeine identity. The supplied spectrum is illustrative, not an authentic reference match.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
Combine independent dimensions of evidence

For a singly protonated molecule, [M+H]⁺ is about one mass unit above neutral M. Fragments and multiple charges require interpretation.Retention, suitable ion evidence, standards and blanks can strengthen an assignment.

More dimensions still require validated interpretation. Quantification needs calibration in addition to identity evidence.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
Write an auditable conclusion

Accepted preparations give 150 and 400 mg/L original caffeine; bars show limited scaled standard uncertainties.What is supported, what is withheld, and what action is needed?

Expected supported values are one hundred fifty and four hundred mg/L under the model. Drink C needs improved separation; C2 is superseded by a valid new preparation.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
Render without hidden session state

The result applies to a defined material under a defined procedure; the signal alone does not define the measurand.Start from original data, saved code and preparation records.

A peer should render from a fresh folder. Missing files, absolute paths or console-only objects reveal a portability failure.

title: Choosing and defending a result
section: Transfer the evidence, not just the equation
text:
Transfer the evidence, not just the equation

The independent final-case line is area equals four plus forty times caffeine concentration, over zero to thirty mg/L.Area 804; 4.00 mL to 40.00 mL; accepted separation and QC.

Final concentration twenty mg/L; original two hundred mg/L. If an unresolved second absorber contributes, withhold the simple caffeine interpretation.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
What would change your decision?

Different analytical questions call for elemental detection, molecular separation, titration or ion-activity measurement.Name the additional chemical or measurement evidence required.

Ask for specific next steps, not just more data: new dilution, better separation, appropriate reference material, recovery study or validated uncertainty component.

title: GC and HPLC
section: Both methods separate; their mobile phases differ
text:
Both methods separate; their mobile phases differ

Different analytical questions call for elemental detection, molecular separation, titration or ion-activity measurement.Can the analyte enter, survive and separate under the method conditions?

Begin with the analyte, matrix and required result, not a preference for an instrument.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Follow the GC sample

The analyte must tolerate introduction and separation conditions. Oven temperature programming changes retention during the run.Carrier gas → inlet → column in oven → detector.

The analyte must reach the gas phase under the chosen conditions without an unacceptable loss or transformation.

title: GC and HPLC
section: Volatility is about the introduced analyte
text:
Volatility is about the introduced analyte

The analyte must tolerate introduction and separation conditions. Oven temperature programming changes retention during the run.A headspace method can sample volatiles above a nonvolatile matrix.

The entire original material need not be volatile. Introduction and sampling partitioning still determine what the result represents.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Temperature programming changes retention

The analyte must tolerate introduction and separation conditions. Oven temperature programming changes retention during the run.Stationary-phase interactions also matter.

Retention order is not a pure boiling-point list. The oven program belongs to the complete GC method.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Follow the HPLC sample

In reversed-phase HPLC, changing organic modifier often changes retention. Re-equilibrate before the next injection.Reservoir → controlled flow and injection → column → detector.

The solute must be soluble and stable under the selected liquid-phase conditions.

title: GC and HPLC
section: Reversed-phase conditions provide one interaction regime
text:
Reversed-phase conditions provide one interaction regime

In reversed-phase HPLC, changing organic modifier often changes retention. Re-equilibrate before the next injection.A relatively nonpolar stationary phase meets a more polar mobile phase.

Organic modifier often reduces retention for appropriately retained compounds. Ionisation and solvent chemistry can alter behaviour, so avoid an absolute rule.

title: GC and HPLC
section: Isocratic and gradient methods ask different practical questions
text:
Isocratic and gradient methods ask different practical questions

An illustrative HPLC program rises from ten to seventy percent organic, then returns and re-equilibrates.A gradient changes composition during a run.

An isocratic method holds it fixed. Gradients can address a broad retention range but need appropriate equilibration and control.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Return to the initial conditions

An illustrative HPLC program rises from ten to seventy percent organic, then returns and re-equilibrates.Which part prepares the next injection?

The program returns to ten percent organic and holds for re-equilibration. Repeating a run without matching the starting state can change retention.

title: GC and HPLC
section: A detector is part of the selectivity
text:
A detector is part of the selectivity

In reversed-phase HPLC, changing organic modifier often changes retention. Re-equilibrate before the next injection.UV, flame-ionisation and mass-spectrometric responses are different.

UV needs absorption at the chosen wavelength; FID gives ion current for many organics; MS records ions by m/z. An area is method-dependent.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Calibrate the integrated area

External HPLC calibration maps caffeine peak area to final-solution concentration from zero to forty mg/L.Known caffeine in final solution: 0–40 mg/L.

Assume suitable baseline and separation under the teaching conditions. Do not count CSV rows as area.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Interpret the external model

External HPLC calibration maps caffeine peak area to final-solution concentration from zero to forty mg/L.Area = 3 + 50 × concentration.

The offset is retained. The model maps response to final-solution concentration, not directly to the original beverage.

title: GC and HPLC
section: What if the injection introduces less solution?
text:
What if the injection introduces less solution?

Repeated injections give external estimates of fifteen and twelve mg/L, but ratio estimates near fifteen mg/L for both.External area can change even when vial concentration does not.

Use repeated injections I1 and I2 of the same preparation D1. Their external estimates are fifteen and twelve mg/L.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Add a distinguishable internal standard

The ratio cannot repair coelution, analyte loss before standard addition, or different behaviour of analyte and standard.Every final solution here has 10 mg/L internal standard.

The compound must be distinguishable from native analyte and matrix, and suitable for the effects it is intended to follow.

title: GC and HPLC
section: A ratio can cancel a shared factor
text:
A ratio can cancel a shared factor

The ratio cannot repair coelution, analyte loss before standard addition, or different behaviour of analyte and standard.If both areas change proportionally, their ratio changes much less.

This is conditional on shared response behaviour and no interfering integrated peaks. It is not a universal correction.

title: GC and HPLC
section: Calibrate the ratio under matched standard concentration
text:
Calibrate the ratio under matched standard concentration

Caffeine-to-internal-standard area ratio is linear in concentration when internal-standard concentration is held fixed.\(R=A_{caffeine}/A_{IS}=0.006+0.100c\).

Fixed IS concentration makes ratio versus analyte concentration appropriate here. Varying IS concentrations require a concentration-ratio model.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Reuse the familiar model fit
fit_ratio <- lm(area_ratio ~ caffeine_mg_l, data = standards)

The principal learning is the experimental design and interpretation, not a new modelling package.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Compare the repeated injections

Repeated injections give external estimates of fifteen and twelve mg/L, but ratio estimates near fifteen mg/L for both.Ratio estimates: 15.000 and 15.015 mg/L final.

The shared injection effect mostly cancels. A small difference remains because the teaching signals include an offset.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Return to the original drink

The ratio cannot repair coelution, analyte loss before standard addition, or different behaviour of analyte and standard.A tenfold dilution gives approximately 150 mg/L original.

These are repeated injections, not independent preparations or drinks. Do not turn two injections into two independently obtained samples.

title: GC and HPLC
section: A late standard cannot report an early loss
text:
A late standard cannot report an early loss

Added analyte may not behave like native bound analyte. A successful late spike cannot establish complete extraction of native material.When was the internal standard added?

If it was added after extraction, it cannot establish the recovery of native caffeine through extraction. Even early addition requires equivalent behaviour.

title: GC and HPLC
section: A ratio cannot repair overlapping peaks
text:
A ratio cannot repair overlapping peaks

The same component areas appear resolved or overlapping when their retention-time spacing changes.An interfering compound can contaminate the analyte or standard area.

I3 has unresolved separation and is withheld despite an algebraically calculable ratio.

title: GC and HPLC
section: A ratio cannot make failed QC disappear
text:
A ratio cannot make failed QC disappear

A blank, independent reference check and a sample spike examine different parts of the measurement.I4 belongs to an unsatisfactory QC condition.

Withhold and investigate. Do not report the value simply because the peak and ratio fall inside the nominal calibration range.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Encode the reporting decision
reportable <- resolved & qc_pass & in_range

The flags must reflect actual separation and QC records. They are not arbitrary switches that make a desired answer reportable.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Choose between plausible methods

Different analytical questions call for elemental detection, molecular separation, titration or ion-activity measurement.Volatile solvent mixture versus a heat-sensitive, nonvolatile aqueous mixture.

GC is a plausible starting point for the solvent mixture; LC for the nonvolatile heat-sensitive compounds. Matrix, stability and detector requirements may refine the choice.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Transfer the ratio calibration

Caffeine-to-internal-standard area ratio is linear in concentration when internal-standard concentration is held fixed.Areas 903 and 600; same IS concentration; original dilution factor 5.

Ratio 1.505; final caffeine 14.99 mg/L; original 74.95 mg/L. Ask why coelution would invalidate the calculation.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
section: A voltage belongs to a cell
text:
A voltage belongs to a cell

An indicator electrode and reference electrode contact the same sample and connect to a high-input-impedance meter. There is negligible net measurement current.Which two functions are required?

Indicator and reference electrodes. A combined electrode packages both functions; it does not remove the reference.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
section: The indicator responds; the reference anchors
text:
The indicator responds; the reference anchors

An indicator electrode and reference electrode contact the same sample and connect to a high-input-impedance meter. There is negligible net measurement current.The measured potential also includes the reference and junction.

Changes in either can affect the reading. A voltage is not an intrinsic concentration label.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Why use a high-input-impedance meter?

An indicator electrode and reference electrode contact the same sample and connect to a high-input-impedance meter. There is negligible net measurement current.Read potential with negligible net measurement current.

Contrast with deliberately current-measuring electrochemical methods. Do not imply a potentiometric electrode is a current detector.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Activity gives the thermodynamic response

Activity is dimensionless and related to concentration by an activity coefficient and standard concentration. Matching ionic strength supports calibration transfer.\(a_i=\gamma_i c_i/c^\circ\).

Activity is dimensionless. A concentration calibration transfers only when the activity relationship is appropriate to standards and sample.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Write the logarithmic relationship
\(E=K+(2.303RT/zF)\log_{10} a_i\).

The sign here includes signed ion charge and the chosen potential convention. At twenty-five Celsius the monovalent magnitude is about 59.16 mV per decade.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
section: Anion and cation slopes need a convention
text:
Anion and cation slopes need a convention

Fluoride potential decreases linearly with log concentration, with slope minus 59.10 mV per decade.For this fluoride example, increasing concentration lowers the potential.

Do not infer a chemistry error solely from a sign without checking instrument polarity and cell convention.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Match conditions before using concentration

Activity is dimensionless and related to concentration by an activity coefficient and standard concentration. Matching ionic strength supports calibration transfer.Ionic-strength adjustment helps; it does not remove every interference.

Discuss activity coefficients, complexes and junction changes. The electrode can respond to free species rather than total element.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
pH is already logarithmic

Illustrative pH potential decreases by 59.16 mV per pH unit at 25 degrees Celsius; the cell sets its intercept.\(pH=-\log_{10}a_{H^+}\).

One pH unit is a tenfold activity change. Avoid treating pH itself as an ordinary concentration in mol/L.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Buffers establish the pH calibration

Illustrative pH potential decreases by 59.16 mV per pH unit at 25 degrees Celsius; the cell sets its intercept.Use appropriate buffers and measurement temperature.

The illustrated ideal intercept is not universal. The cell and calibration establish the actual response.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Inspect the fluoride standards

The same fluoride measurements form a curved relationship on an untransformed concentration axis.Range here: 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻³ mol/L at matched conditions.

This is the supplied scenario range, not a universal electrode range or a full validation.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Transform the explanatory quantity
mutate(log_c = log10(fluoride_mol_l))

Numerically this takes concentration in mol/L relative to one mol/L. Zero and negative concentrations cannot be ordinary log-calibration points.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
section: The correct axes reveal the model
text:
The correct axes reveal the model

Fluoride potential decreases linearly with log concentration, with slope minus 59.10 mV per decade.The same observations are nearly linear against log concentration.

Ask why a straight line on the untransformed concentration axis would be inappropriate.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Read the slope per decade

Fluoride potential decreases linearly with log concentration, with slope minus 59.10 mV per decade.Fitted slope = −59.10 mV per decade.

A factor of ten in concentration is a one-unit change on the explanatory axis. The fitted intercept is about minus 97.42 mV.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Invert in two steps
First \((E-a)/b\); then \(c=10^{(E-a)/b}\) mol/L.

For the measured 121.2 mV, the exponent is about minus 3.699. Forgetting the power of ten leaves a log value rather than concentration.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Report the accepted early sample

Fluoride potential decreases linearly with log concentration, with slope minus 59.10 mV per decade.121.2 mV → 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L.

Check that this lies within the supplied calibration range. Identity and matrix compatibility remain assumptions.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
section: Check the calibration at a known concentration
text:
Check the calibration at a known concentration

The early fluoride check has error 0.12 mV and passes; the later check has error 6.02 mV and fails the two-mV tolerance.The check is 1.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L; exercise tolerance ±2.0 mV.

The expected response is 138.98 mV. The check is separate from merely asking whether the fit is straight.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
The early block passes

The early fluoride check has error 0.12 mV and passes; the later check has error 6.02 mV and fails the two-mV tolerance.Observed 139.1 mV; error +0.12 mV.

Use the preselected rule. Do not re-estimate a tolerance after observing the data.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
The later block fails

The early fluoride check has error 0.12 mV and passes; the later check has error 6.02 mV and fails the two-mV tolerance.Observed 145.0 mV; error +6.02 mV.

Withhold the affected later sample. Investigate, establish satisfactory calibration and checks, then remeasure.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
section: A drift does not identify its cause
text:
A drift does not identify its cause

An indicator electrode and reference electrode contact the same sample and connect to a high-input-impedance meter. There is negligible net measurement current.Conditioning, junction, temperature and matrix changes are candidates.

The graph alone does not establish which occurred. Avoid automatically subtracting the observed check error from every later sample.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
section: Uncertainty changes shape through the inverse
text:
Uncertainty changes shape through the inverse

Fluoride potential decreases linearly with log concentration, with slope minus 59.10 mV per decade.Symmetric voltage limits can become asymmetric concentration limits.

Exponentiation maps additive voltage uncertainty into multiplicative concentration uncertainty. Never attach a voltage SD directly to a concentration result.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Place other electrochemical signals
Potential: potentiometry. Current: amperometry or voltammetry. Charge: coulometry.

Different signals need different measurement models. Coulometric amount additionally requires the intended reaction to account for the charge.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Transfer: a 17.8 mV decrease

Fluoride potential decreases linearly with log concentration, with slope minus 59.10 mV per decade.Predict the concentration factor before calculating.

With slope minus 59.10, factor is about 2.001. The accepted estimate becomes about four times ten to minus four mol/L.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Would this measure total fluorine?

Activity is dimensionless and related to concentration by an activity coefficient and standard concentration. Matching ionic strength supports calibration transfer.Free-ion response does not automatically include every chemical form.

Ask what preparation and speciation evidence would be needed. Return to the measurand rather than treating the instrument name as the answer.

title: Sampling and preparation
section: Precision cannot rescue an unrepresentative sample
text:
Precision cannot rescue an unrepresentative sample

Equal-mass top, middle and bottom strata have different iron concentrations. Top-only sampling is biased.Where would you take material from this container?

Ask students to state the target quantity before choosing grabs. Equal stratum masses are given for the example.

title: Sampling and preparation
text:
Look within and between positions

Iron averages 8, 14 and 25 mg/kg in equal-mass top, middle and bottom strata, with small within-stratum scatter.Which variation dominates?

Top means eight, middle fourteen, bottom twenty-five mg/kg. The within-position variation is much smaller.

title: Sampling and preparation
text:
Define the sampling target

Equal-mass top, middle and bottom strata have different iron concentrations. Top-only sampling is biased.Bulk mean, spatial variation and maximum are different questions.

A single composite may be suitable for one question but erase information needed for another.

title: Sampling and preparation
section: Weight the material you mean to represent
text:
Weight the material you mean to represent

Equal-mass top, middle and bottom strata have different iron concentrations. Top-only sampling is biased.Equal masses: \((8+14+25)/3=15.67\) mg/kg.

If masses differ, use their known fractions. A simple mean across arbitrary grabs need not be a bulk mass mean.

title: Sampling and preparation
section: More top-only grabs repeat the same mistake
text:
More top-only grabs repeat the same mistake

Iron averages 8, 14 and 25 mg/kg in equal-mass top, middle and bottom strata, with small within-stratum scatter.A small SD can coexist with a large sampling bias.

The top-only mean remains about eight mg/kg. Repetition is useful only within a design that addresses the target.

title: Sampling and preparation
section: A composite is one combined material
text:
A composite is one combined material

Equal-mass top, middle and bottom strata have different iron concentrations. Top-only sampling is biased.Combining increments does not create independent collected samples.

Ask what is lost when all positions are combined. One composite cannot estimate spatial variability by itself.

title: Sampling and preparation
section: Storage can change what reaches the instrument
text:
Storage can change what reaches the instrument

Storage can change composition by reactions, adsorption or biological processes. Preservation is method dependent.Which process could change an oxidation-state result?

Oxidation can change species. Adsorption can remove dissolved analyte. Biological changes can alter several chemical quantities.

title: Sampling and preparation
text:
Preservation must fit the measurand

Storage can change composition by reactions, adsorption or biological processes. Preservation is method dependent.An acid treatment can preserve an elemental amount while changing chemical form.

Do not offer a universal preservation recipe. The approved method specifies container, treatment, time and other relevant conditions.

title: Sampling and preparation
text:
Filtration, extraction and digestion differ

1.92 × (10/2) × 0.025 = 0.240 mg extracted caffeine; 0.240 / 0.5000 = 0.480 mg/g.A clear solution is not proof of complete analyte recovery.

Filtration separates material; extraction transfers accessible solute; digestion breaks down material. Each changes the interpretation of the result.

title: Sampling and preparation
text:
Keep the whole preparation chain

1.92 × (10/2) × 0.025 = 0.240 mg extracted caffeine; 0.240 / 0.5000 = 0.480 mg/g.What unit belongs at each stage?

Dry material has a mass basis. Extract and final solution have mass-per-volume bases. Ask students to identify each quantity before calculating.

title: Sampling and preparation
text:
Begin at the measured flask

1.92 × (10/2) × 0.025 = 0.240 mg extracted caffeine; 0.240 / 0.5000 = 0.480 mg/g.T1a final concentration: 1.92 mg caffeine/L.

The final flask is ten millilitres containing a two-millilitre extract aliquot. This is not yet caffeine per gram.

title: Sampling and preparation
text:
Undo the aliquot dilution

1.92 × (10/2) × 0.025 = 0.240 mg extracted caffeine; 0.240 / 0.5000 = 0.480 mg/g.1.92 × 10.00/2.00 = 9.60 mg/L extract.

Use final total volume, including reagents and solvent. Explain why the factor multiplies when returning to the more concentrated extract.

title: Sampling and preparation
text:
Recover extracted amount

1.92 × (10/2) × 0.025 = 0.240 mg extracted caffeine; 0.240 / 0.5000 = 0.480 mg/g.9.60 mg/L × 0.02500 L = 0.240 mg.

Cancel litres. Ask what thousand-fold error would occur if twenty-five millilitres were used as twenty-five litres.

title: Sampling and preparation
section: Report on the original material basis
text:
Report on the original material basis

Extracted caffeine results of 0.480, 0.490 and 0.750 mg/g for three identified preparations.0.240 mg / 0.5000 g = 0.480 mg/g.

Call this extracted caffeine. Complete recovery of native caffeine has not been independently established.

title: Sampling and preparation
text:
Keep preparation identities

Extracted caffeine results of 0.480, 0.490 and 0.750 mg/g for three identified preparations.T1a and T1b are two preparations of T1.

Do not call the three preparations three independent supplied materials. The table contains two preparations of T1 and one of T2.

title: Sampling and preparation
section: Write the mass balance in R
text:
Write the mass balance in R
mutate(extract_mg_l = final_caffeine_mg_l * final_ml / aliquot_ml,
       extracted_mg = extract_mg_l * extract_ml / 1000,
       caffeine_mg_g = extracted_mg / mass_g)

Read one expression chemically. The factor of one thousand converts millilitres to litres; it is not an empirical correction.

title: Sampling and preparation
section: Partitioning depends on concentrations and volumes
text:
Partitioning depends on concentrations and volumes

Two immiscible phases share analyte at distribution ratio nine. The organic ten millilitres holds 81.8 percent of the mass.\(D=c_o/c_a\); analyte amount exists in both phases.

The distribution ratio is nine in this ideal example. Concentration ratio alone is not recovery.

title: Sampling and preparation
section: Recover the fraction from a mass balance
text:
Recover the fraction from a mass balance

Two immiscible phases share analyte at distribution ratio nine. The organic ten millilitres holds 81.8 percent of the mass.\(f_o=DV_o/(V_a+DV_o)\).

With twenty millilitres aqueous and ten millilitres extracting solvent, the recovered fraction is ninety over one hundred ten, or 81.8 percent.

title: Sampling and preparation
section: Use the same total solvent differently
text:
Use the same total solvent differently

Ideal recovery rises from 81.8 percent for one 10 mL extraction to 90.5 percent for two 5 mL extractions.One 10 mL extraction: 81.8%. Two 5 mL extractions: 90.5%.

For successive extractions multiply the fractions left behind, assuming equilibration and complete phase separation each time.

title: Sampling and preparation
text:
Recognise the idealisation

Two immiscible phases share analyte at distribution ratio nine. The organic ten millilitres holds 81.8 percent of the mass.What could invalidate the simple partition calculation?

Emulsions, incomplete equilibrium, changing phase volumes, chemical reaction, ionisation or binding can alter the distribution and recovery.

title: Sampling and preparation
section: A late spike misses early losses
text:
A late spike misses early losses

Added analyte may not behave like native bound analyte. A successful late spike cannot establish complete extraction of native material.Adding analyte after extraction cannot establish extraction recovery.

Native bound analyte may behave differently even from a pre-extraction spike. State the point of addition and the equivalence assumption.

title: Sampling and preparation
text:
Transfer the volume chain

1.92 × (10/2) × 0.025 = 0.240 mg extracted caffeine; 0.240 / 0.5000 = 0.480 mg/g.0.4000 g → 40.00 mL extract → 1.00 mL to 10.00 mL → 1.50 mg/L.

Give time to derive 1.50 mg/g extracted caffeine. Ask what extra evidence would justify total caffeine.

title: Sampling and preparation
section: Choose an improvement that addresses the failure
text:
Choose an improvement that addresses the failure
Would you change sampling, extraction, or repeat readings?

Use three cases: top-only bias, incomplete extraction, noisy stable readings. Match the intervention to the source instead of assuming more instrument replicates solve everything.

title: Equilibrium and titration
section: A known reagent counts an unknown amount
text:
A known reagent counts an unknown amount

A burette delivers standardised titrant to a known sample aliquot. Endpoint detection estimates the stoichiometric equivalence point.What makes delivered volume chemically meaningful?

Known titrant concentration and reaction stoichiometry. The indicator or electrode estimates the endpoint; it does not replace the reaction.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Know the titrant concentration
A nominal concentration is not automatically a standardised concentration.

The example supplies standardised 0.1000 mol/L base. Real preparation and standardisation uncertainty belong in the result.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Read delivered volume

A burette delivers standardised titrant to a known sample aliquot. Endpoint detection estimates the stoichiometric equivalence point.Delivered volume = final reading − initial reading.

An initial position need not be zero. Ask students what a burette reading records and why the final reading alone can be misleading.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Separate equivalence from endpoint

A burette delivers standardised titrant to a known sample aliquot. Endpoint detection estimates the stoichiometric equivalence point.Equivalence is stoichiometric. The endpoint is observed or estimated.

An indicator, electrode or algorithm gives a procedure-defined estimate. Explain endpoint bias using a systematic overrun.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Write the reaction first
\(\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}\). One mole consumes one mole.

The concentration formula follows from the one-to-one stoichiometry. Other stoichiometries need their coefficients, not a memorised volume shortcut.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Calculate a worked acid concentration

Ideal strong-acid titration pH rises sharply near 25 mL base added; equivalence pH is seven at 25 degrees Celsius.\(c_a=c_b V_{eq}/V_a\) = 0.1000 × 25.00/25.00 = 0.1000 mol/L.

The acid aliquot is 25.00 mL. Supplied endpoint estimate is 25.00 mL. Explain when volumes may remain in matching millilitre units and when mole calculations require litres.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Explain the curve before equivalence

Ideal strong-acid titration pH rises sharply near 25 mL base added; equivalence pH is seven at 25 degrees Celsius.What species mainly determines pH here?

Excess strong acid. The ideal model also includes water equilibrium; it matters near equivalence.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Explain the curve after equivalence

Ideal strong-acid titration pH rises sharply near 25 mL base added; equivalence pH is seven at 25 degrees Celsius.What now controls pH?

Excess strong base. The total volume is changing, so excess amount is divided by the current solution volume.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Neutrality is conditional

Ideal strong-acid titration pH rises sharply near 25 mL base added; equivalence pH is seven at 25 degrees Celsius.This ideal strong-acid/strong-base equivalence has pH 7 at 25 °C.

It is not a universal endpoint rule. A weak acid will provide a counterexample.

title: Equilibrium and titration
section: Differentiate using the actual volume spacing
text:
Differentiate using the actual volume spacing

Finite-difference pH slope peaks close to 25 mL, with the actual addition spacing included.Finite difference: \(\Delta pH/\Delta V\).

The supplied table has smaller additions near equivalence. Treating every step as one millilitre distorts the derivative.

title: Equilibrium and titration
section: A numerical maximum is not complete validation
text:
A numerical maximum is not complete validation

Finite-difference pH slope peaks close to 25 mL, with the actual addition spacing included.Noise and step spacing affect the slope peak.

Use the exploratory derivative to locate a region. A real endpoint method must be specified and evaluated against the chemical question.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Same amount, different equilibrium

Strong and weak acids have the same equivalence volume here but different pH curves and indicator requirements.Which acid requires more base at equivalence?

They have the same initial amount and one-to-one stoichiometry, so the equivalence volumes are equal. Acid strength changes the curve, not the supplied amount.

title: Equilibrium and titration
section: Choose an indicator for the actual curve
text:
Choose an indicator for the actual curve

Strong and weak acids have the same equivalence volume here but different pH curves and indicator requirements.A transition interval must lie in an appropriate steep region.

For the weak acid, conjugate base affects equivalence pH. Do not choose an indicator solely because its colour is easy to see.

title: Equilibrium and titration
section: The buffer region has a chemical cause
text:
The buffer region has a chemical cause

Strong and weak acids have the same equivalence volume here but different pH curves and indicator requirements.Weak acid and its conjugate base coexist before equivalence.

The comparison weak acid has supplied pKa 4.76. No exhaustive polyprotic derivation is needed for the core task.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
EDTA gives another stoichiometric count

Buffer and indicator support the selected titration. Hardness as CaCO₃ is an equivalent reporting basis, not a claim that CaCO₃ was dissolved.One accessible metal ion consumes one EDTA ligand.

The simplified hardness case counts accessible calcium and magnesium. Other metals can interfere if they also consume EDTA.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
pH changes effective binding

Buffer and indicator support the selected titration. Hardness as CaCO₃ is an equivalent reporting basis, not a claim that CaCO₃ was dissolved.Ligand protonation and metal side reactions affect the conditional equilibrium.

A large overall formation constant is not sufficient to establish performance under arbitrary acidity. Buffer and indicator belong to the procedure.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Name the reporting basis

Buffer and indicator support the selected titration. Hardness as CaCO₃ is an equivalent reporting basis, not a claim that CaCO₃ was dissolved.Hardness as CaCO₃ uses an equivalent molar mass.

It does not establish that carbonate was present or separately identify calcium and magnesium. We supply molar mass 100.09 g/mol.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Correct the measured consumption

A burette delivers standardised titrant to a known sample aliquot. Endpoint detection estimates the stoichiometric equivalence point.H1a: 6.30 − 0.10 − 0.05 = 6.15 mL.

The first two numbers are final and initial burette positions. The third is matched blank consumption, on the same delivered-volume basis.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Calculate the metal amount

Buffer and indicator support the selected titration. Hardness as CaCO₃ is an equivalent reporting basis, not a claim that CaCO₃ was dissolved.0.01000 mol/L × 0.00615 L = 6.15 × 10⁻⁵ mol.

This amount refers to the 50.00 mL sample aliquot. Retain full precision and convert to the reporting equivalent only after establishing amount.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Convert to the sample basis

Three preparations give about 123, 124 and 191 mg/L hardness as calcium carbonate.6.15 × 10⁻⁵ mol × 100.09 g/mol / 0.05000 L = 123.11 mg/L as CaCO₃.

Show the gram-to-milligram conversion explicitly in discussion.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Keep repeated preparations distinct

Three preparations give about 123, 124 and 191 mg/L hardness as calcium carbonate.H1a and H1b are separate preparations of H1.

They probe preparation repeatability; they are not independent collected waters. H2a is another supplied sample.

title: Equilibrium and titration
section: What can bias a titration result?
text:
What can bias a titration result?

A burette delivers standardised titrant to a known sample aliquot. Endpoint detection estimates the stoichiometric equivalence point.Endpoint overrun, wrong titrant concentration, blank consumption, interference.

Ask for the direction of error for one example. A forgotten positive blank consumption raises the result in this model.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Transfer the reaction and basis

Buffer and indicator support the selected titration. Hardness as CaCO₃ is an equivalent reporting basis, not a claim that CaCO₃ was dissolved.25.00 mL water; 4.10 mL delivered EDTA; 0.10 mL blank; 0.01000 mol/L.

Allow the calculation. Corrected four millilitres yields 160.14 mg/L as CaCO3. Require the reporting basis in the answer.
